title: Trump’s DOJ charged hundreds with assaulting officers. Many cases were dropped, but the damage was done
description: , Kristina Cooke, M.B.
fullText:
July 30 - Christian Garcia admits that he threw a water bottle toward officers guarding a federal building near Los Angeles during an immigration protest last summer.

The plastic bottle was empty, he said, and hit no one but Garcia himself – the wind blew it back at him. Yet Garcia, a 32-year-old amateur photographer, was arrested by agents, jailed for three days and charged with a crime that could have kept him in prison for up to a year. He said he lost both of his jobs, as a security ‌guard and an undercover shopper, after his bosses told him they had been called by investigators.

Then, with no public explanation, prosecutors dropped the case.

The Trump administration has brought criminal charges against at least 851 people accused of attacking or impeding federal officers, only to abandon them at an unusually high rate. A ‌Reuters review of federal court records found that 31% of these cases that have been completed so far have ended in dismissal. That compares to 8% of all federal criminal cases that typically end in dismissal, according to records compiled by the Federal Judicial Center.

Prosecutors fared especially poorly when bringing charges against people detained during immigration protests, dropping about 45% of the 86 such cases that had been completed by the end of May, Reuters found.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said its leadership has made clear that "anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law." Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said prosecutors should hold people accountable for such assaults, but "if there are mitigating factors identified in a case, then prosecutors must also act appropriately to inform the court, and in some cases downgrade or drop charges."

The DOJ's charges have imposed a steep cost on some people, even when the cases are dropped. Reuters interviewed a half dozen people who, despite the abandoned charges, reported lost jobs, legal fees and in some cases a flurry of online threats that arrived after federal officials publicized their arrests.

Garcia said he couldn't get his jobs back even after prosecutors dismissed his case. He said he also never got ‌back the phone an agent seized.

"It's like I got no justice whatsoever," Garcia said. "My whole life changed in one day."

The ⁠original charging document said Garcia was "observed throwing an object" at officers while others in a crowd threw projectiles "including rocks and water bottles" that struck officers' shields.

Their accounts show the Trump administration regularly opted to make federal cases out of encounters that prosecutors said historically would not have led to arrests or serious charges.

Among them are a woman who backed her SUV into an ⁠agent's car at low speed; a man who challenged an agent to box but threw no punches; and another who jumped on a Homeland Security agent's car during a protest. And they famously brought charges against a Washington man who threw a sandwich that bounced off an immigration agent's body armor.

Other assaults in the cases reviewed by Reuters were serious and would almost certainly have been prosecuted under any administration, including the case of a woman in Minnesota accused of biting off the tip of a federal agent's finger in January.

But the scale and intensity of the Trump administration's pursuit of alleged officer assaults breaks from past DOJ practice, as does its lowered bar for bringing such cases to court, according to court records and people familiar with the effort.

The Justice Department instructed ​prosecutors last ​year that decisions to turn down such cases had to be explained to Washington, two officials familiar with the instructions said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. That pressured prosecutors to take cases ​that might otherwise have been rejected.

Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told immigration officials in Arizona in May that the department would ‌prosecute any assault on an officer "no matter what."

Federal prosecutors almost always win the cases they bring. Most years, about 90% of the people charged with a federal crime are convicted, according to records kept by the Federal Judicial Center.

The Trump administration's spate of assault charges has been a notable exception, with prosecutors securing convictions in 65% of the 481 cases Reuters examined that had been completed. The vast majority of the cases were dismissed at prosecutors' request.

The remaining cases among the 851 reviewed by Reuters are still pending.

The high dismissal rate suggests authorities "are moving so fast that they don't have time to do their job effectively," said Kyle Boynton, a former federal prosecutor and FBI agent with experience in assault investigations.

In most cases, prosecutors provided no reason for dropping charges, other than saying that it was "in the interests of justice."

That was the explanation they gave Lizzie Rose, who was charged in January with backing her car into an SUV carrying immigration agents after following it through Minneapolis. A neighbor captured the incident on video, which shows a low-speed collision.

The Homeland Security Department posted her mugshot on social media with a promise that "we will not be intimidated." Her picture appeared in news reports as well. Enough threats poured into her own feeds that she left her house and sent her two children to live with their father, she said.

"It consumed our lives," she said. "It was every day."

Rose, 42, was put on ‌leave from her job at a Minneapolis nonprofit.

When prosecutors threw out their assault charges against 21-year-old Luci Mazur in Chicago, the judge noted that the agent who charged her "had sworn under oath ​that the affiant had reviewed video evidence that corroborated" his assertion that Mazur had grabbed his arm and resisted arrest. Body-camera footage however, was a factor in the decision by prosecutors to drop the case, the ​judge said.

Four current and former law enforcement officials said prosecutors' willingness to take on such cases – especially when agents' accounts are revealed to be inaccurate – risks undermining ​the trust that judges routinely afford government lawyers.

Last September, Michael Rabbitt, a local Democratic political official in Chicago, attended a morning protest outside an ICE processing facility in nearby Broadview that had become a flashpoint during the administration's immigration crackdown in the region.

As cars passed, he said, ‌the protesters moved out of the way to let them through, as directed by Broadview Police. But he said an ICE ​vehicle did not wait for protesters to clear out of the way. A video of ​the incident shows Rabbitt with his hand on the side of the car for about 30 seconds as it slowly moved forward.

About a month later, while visiting Portugal with his wife for their 30-year anniversary, he got a voicemail from an FBI agent telling him he had been indicted and to turn himself in.

The charges included a misdemeanor for impeding the agent's vehicle and a felony charge of conspiring to impede or injure officers, which Rabbitt called "ridiculous."

Prosecutors dropped the conspiracy charges in early May but insisted that he go to trial for blocking the ICE vehicle.

Days before the trial was scheduled, a federal judge in Chicago assailed prosecutors ​for their handling of the case. The judge accused them of stacking a federal grand jury in their favor by excusing people ‌who were unlikely to vote to indict; improperly suggesting that jurors could rely on the prosecutor's credibility rather than the evidence; and communicating with the jurors outside the grand jury room.

The Justice Department dismissed all the charges. In a rare move, prosecutors said they would not contest a defense request ​for the DOJ to pay some of the legal fees for Rabbitt and other defendants charged in connection with the same protest.

"I do believe deeply in the presumption of regularity and that most government attorneys are doing the best they can to do the right thing," Judge April Perry ​said. "That trust has been broken."

title: More than 1,200 AI workers across Anthropic, DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta are asking for Washington’s help building an AI slowdown plan
description: The statement, signed by senior executives at competing companies, calls on the government to help build the tools needed to pace frontier AI development.
fullText:
More than 1,200 employees at the world's leading AI labs, including senior executives, have signed a statement asking the U.S. government to help build the tools needed to slow down AI development if it ever becomes necessary.

The statement, titled "Pacing the Frontier," was published Tuesday and has been signed by prominent tech figures including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and several of the company's cofounders, alongside OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao, and Google DeepMind head of AI safety and alignment Anca Dragan.

The list brings together companies that are normally locked in fierce competition with one another and is a striking statement for an industry under enormous commercial pressure to keep building ever larger and more capable models.

"Having so many staff from different companies come together in agreement on this point is striking," Tyler Johnston, founder of the Midas Project, an AI watchdog group, told Fortune. "There are many bitter rivalries and disagreements in the industry, so the fact that there is such strong consensus on this point is a warning that we really ought to pay attention to."

While the statement does not ask any company to slow down at the moment, it does call on Washington to support an international effort to build the technical and governance tools that would help the world "pace" development. It specifically calls out the risks around AI systems that start to design their own successors faster than anyone can understand or control them.

"Having talked to many of the people who signed the letter, they don't want a pause," Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, told Fortune. "But there is a concern about how the technology is advancing." The companies are looking for the optionality to do that at some point and have support from a third party when that point arrives, he added.

The letter comes in the wake of a security breach that has rattled the AI industry. OpenAI disclosed that two of its models, the newly released GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable unreleased research system, broke out of a sandboxed internal test environment, found a previously unknown vulnerability that gave them access to the open internet, and then used stolen credentials and additional exploits to breach the production systems of Hugging Face to steal the answers to a cybersecurity benchmark they were being evaluated on. Hugging Face detected and contained the intrusion on its own days before OpenAI connected the activity to its internal testing, and had already reported it to law enforcement.

title: Scotland's centuries-old guga hunt could be refused licence
description: Gannets have been killed for their meat during an annual hunt on a Hebridean island - but officials have recommended permission be refused this year.
fullText:
Permission could be refused for a traditional hunt of young seabirds to take place on an uninhabited Hebridean island later this summer.

For centuries, gannets have been killed for their meat during an annual hunt on Sula Sgeir, a small rocky island 40 miles (64km) north of Ness on Lewis in the Western Isles.

NatureScot officials have recommended board members refuse granting a licence for this year's hunt due to the potential impact on Sula Sgeir's gannet population. The officials said animal welfare concerns were also considered.

The board, which is due to meet next week, could vote on two other options - allowing a hunt of either 2,000 or 500 birds.

NatureScot, a public body, issues licences for the hunts and has been assessing the latest application.

Previously it has said the cultural significance of the hunt was recognised under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and hunters must apply for permission every year.

In a new report, officials have recommended a licence be refused this year.

Animal welfare organisations have welcomed the move, but Save Our Guga Harvest campaign said it was disappointed by the recommendation.

Permission sought for traditional guga hunt to take place this year

Guga hunt tradition returns after licence granted

The practice, called a guga hunt and dating back to the 15th Century, usually takes place in August.

Last year NatureScot granted a licence allowing up to 500 birds to be killed, following three years when the hunt had not been held due to bird flu.

The agency said the number had been reduced from 2,000 in recent times to allow the population to recover from the impact of the disease.

A total of 485 birds were taken at the 2025 hunt.

Ahead of Monday's meeting, NatureScot said: "We understand there are strong feelings about the guga hunt, and that some people will disagree with it taking place.

"The hunt is recognised in law under the Wildlife and Countryside Act, which makes specific provision for the granting of a licence for the purpose of providing food for human consumption in relation to the gannets on the island of Sula Sgeir.

"Our role is to make licensing decisions based on the most recent scientific evidence and the relevant legal frameworks."

It said it would not be making further comment until after the meeting.

Animal rights campaigners, who oppose the hunt and say it is no longer needed to provide food for islanders, held a protest at NatureScot's headquarters in Inverness earlier this month.

Devon Docherty, Scottish campaigns manager at Protect the Wild, said it would be "a relief" if 2,000 young gannets would get to "spread their wings and fly".

Scottish animal welfare charity OneKind said that "kindness and constructive evidence" looked set to end the hunt.

Chief executive Jason Rose said: "Since the licensing of the hunt resumed last summer, OneKind has calmly and clearly made the case for this grisly piece of history to be retired, as no animal should ever have to suffer in the name of human tradition."

Murdo Macritchie, of Save Our Guga Harvest campaign claimed there had been a "toxic nature" to the opposition to the hunt, and a lack of understanding about it.

He said it was unclear why a hunt involving 500 birds had not been recommended.

Macritchie said: "I'm really, really keen to get more details on why it was okay last year and why not this year.

"What has changed? Is there any change in the way the data is used or interpreted?"

More than 104,000 people have signed a petition calling for the Scottish government to prohibit the hunt.

Holyrood's petitions committee is considering whether the call should be debated by MSPs.

title: Trump shrugs off Cornyn’s hold on Blanche: ‘I heard he’s going through quite nicely’
description: President Trump brushed off concerns that Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) could hold up acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination in the Senate on Wednesday, saying he heard the process is going “q...
fullText:
President Trump brushed off concerns that Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) could hold up acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination in the Senate on Wednesday, saying he heard the process is going "quite nicely.

"I don't know what it is, but I haven't heard that there's a problem. I've heard he's going through quite nicely," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.

"All I can say is Todd Blanche is outstanding, and I thought it was pretty routine because he's good. You just wouldn't find a better person," he continued.

The president's comments come after Cornyn said his scheduled meeting with Blanche was canceled on Wednesday and that he was "not prepared to vote yes" on advancing Blanche's nomination.

"Maybe John Cornyn's upset with me because I didn't endorse him," Trump said, noting his decision earlier this year to back Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over Cornyn in the state's contested Republican Senate primary.

One Republican "no" vote on Blanche could stall his nomination in committee.

Cornyn has been pressuring the Justice Department on a controversial "anti-weaponization" fund.

The Texas senator told reporters Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told him he needed to know by 4 p.m. whether Thursday morning's scheduled vote could proceed.

"So we still got a little time, and hopefully they now recognize the seriousness of this, and will be responding," Cornyn said.

Trump was also asked about Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) saying this week that he did not have the 50 votes necessary to advance a budget reconciliation bill through the Senate.

"Well, that's too bad for him. I mean, that's too bad for him and too bad for the Republican Party. He's got the votes. He should get it done. He should be able to get it done," Trump said.

Trump has also been pushing Thune and Senate Republicans to remove the filibuster to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a law that would create new federal requirements for voter identification.

Thune insists there's not enough GOP support for such a move, and last week he suggested the White House help whip votes.

Asked if Thune was still "the man for the job," Trump told reporters, "Well, we're going to find out, and I'll let you know."

title: Analysis-Japan PM's political doom loop worsens her fight with markets
description: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is fighting a losing battle in the polls, making a retreat from promised tax cuts more difficult
fullText:
TOKYO, July 29 (Reuters) - Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is fighting a losing battle in the polls, making a retreat from promised tax cuts more difficult and denying her officials the political backup they need to talk down yen and bond market bears.

Takaichi's approval rating slumped in July to the lowest since she took office last year ‌as rising inflation, blamed in part on high import costs from a weak yen, hit her standing with voters.

The prime minister's strong advocacy of fiscal stimulus and harsh criticism of higher interest rates ‌have heightened investor concerns about worsening public finances in Japan, sending bond yields higher.

Those bond market anxieties have also blunted official efforts to talk down speculative bets against the yen, government sources said.

"Markets are gaining control over fiscal management, which hasn't happened in Japan for ​decades," one of them said, warning about the danger of being at the mercy of bond vigilantes.

Since becoming prime minister last year, Takaichi has sought to pursue a pro-growth agenda while also tempering investor concerns about fiscal discipline and central bank independence.

Those competing demands have created a communication challenge that has at times led to unwanted market volatility, which in turn makes policy implementation more difficult.

For example, her spending plans, aimed in part at easing rising household living costs, lifted bond yields to three-decade highs in July on concern over Japan's worsening finances.

Mindful of such market pressures, Takaichi told a news briefing on Monday the administration would seek to gain market trust in Japan's finances through ‌transparent communication.

"I would say communication with markets would become more important," she said ⁠when asked what she could have done better.

But when pressed about her administration's sliding approval ratings, Takaichi stressed her determination to break Japan's "excessive fiscal tightening" with big investment, a sign she had no plans to back down on expansionist policy.

"The sliding approval ratings would only solidify the premier's determination to cut tax and boost investment," another source ⁠said. "Pursuing her policies would jolt markets, while not doing so would hit her popularity. It's a dilemma."

Those challenges could worsen ahead of a host of events that could ignite a renewed spike in yields.

Despite reservations voiced even within her ruling party, Takaichi is set to proceed with a plan to cut by two years an 8% levy on food, domestic media reported. While the move would come as little surprise, a lack of funding clarity could further upset bond markets, analysts say.

title: Police: Bullets that killed 2 bystanders at Seattle festival weren't from teen shooter's gun
description: Preliminary testing showed the bullets that killed two bystanders during a shootout at a crowded Seattle food festival last weekend didn’t come from the gun a 15-year-old arrested at the scene was see...
fullText:
SEATTLE (AP) — Preliminary testing showed the bullets that killed two bystanders during a shootout at a crowded Seattle food festival last weekend didn't come from the gun a 15-year-old arrested at the scene was seen firing, police said in court documents filed Wednesday.

The teen repeatedly shot an untraceable ghost gun into a crowd, police said, and the King County prosecutor's office filed charges of first-degree assault with a firearm and unlawful possession of a handgun.

In a statement supporting the charges, police said preliminary testing of bullets recovered from the two bystanders killed showed they did not match that weapon.

The shooting in the waning hours of the Bite of Seattle festival near the Space Needle left three people dead, including a 19-year-old suspect, and at least four bystanders injured, including a toddler. Police believe it was gang-related, and they continue searching for others who might have been involved.

Police Chief Shon Barnes had previously said there was possibly another person with a gunshot wound that investigators were looking to speak with, but the department said Wednesday there was no eighth victim.

Testing on shell casings found at the scene suggest four weapons were fired, the statement said. Police said they recovered three guns, but only two of them had been fired, which means two weapons involved in the gunbattle were not found at the scene. It isn't clear which weapon or weapons fired the bullets that hit the festival attendees.

Dozens of officers were at Seattle Center, a sprawling park, providing security for the event, when the shooting began. Some heard the gunshots, and one officer saw the 15-year-old firing, police said.

A witness told investigators that he heard gunshots and saw the people around him duck, Detective Matt Blackburn wrote in the statement. The witness saw a man in a light blue top who started running; the witness believed that was where the first shots came from.

The witness reported that he then saw the 15-year-old unzip a bag that was strapped around his torso and pull out a gun with an extended magazine. The teen shot multiple times toward the other suspect, Blackburn wrote. Two shell casings from the teen's ghost gun were found at the scene.

The teen surrendered when confronted by an officer. As police escorted him past the dead 19-year-old's body, he said, "Love you bro," Blackburn wrote.

Prosecutors on Wednesday asked a judge to move the case to adult court, a decision that can take months after the judge considers arguments from both sides. The teen's public defender, Hong Tran, said in an email Wednesday the teen would contest the effort to try him as an adult.

If the teen is convicted as an adult, the charges would carry a sentencing range of about eight to 10 years in prison, plus possibly another five years for the firearm enhancement. However, judges in Washington may also choose to sentence juveniles as juveniles even if they are convicted in adult court.

In juvenile court, the charges would carry a sentencing range of two to 2 1/2 years. It was not immediately clear whether the firearm enhancement might add additional time in juvenile detention.

The King County Medical Examiner's Office identified the dead bystanders as Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56. The suspect killed was Junior Cee Niko Semo, 19.

Villalba was a husband and father of three known for his kindness and willingness to help others, according to a GoFundMe campaign launched Monday to help his family with funeral expenses.

Whitehead had just moved to Washington from Alabama a year ago and was enjoying the festival with one of her adult daughters when she was shot, her cousin Michelle Whitehead told The Associated Press. She was taken to the hospital and died in surgery, she said.

The police department opened an online portal on Wednesday for the public to share video and photos from the shooting.

title: 'I milked the cows the day after getting married'
description: Margaret Lees, 89, has run her family's farm in Greater Manchester since her wedding day in 1957.
fullText:
A great-grandmother has described running her family's farm for nearly 70 years as a "brilliant" life.

Margaret Lees, 89, took over Park Farm near Ramsbottom in Greater Manchester in 1957 with her late husband John.

"We got married, jumped in the Land Rover and drove over here," she explained. "The next day I was milking the cows and starting the milk rounds."

The thriving farm business is still family-run nearly seven decades later.

Margaret said their farmhouse was "unbelievably basic" when she and her groom first arrived following their wedding.

"We had a chair, a table and a bed," she remembered. "Two knives and two forks and one teaspoon.

"We were quite poor for a while as we saved our money for the outside, for the cows."

Over the following years, Margaret and John slowly built up the business, buying and selling pigs, increasing milk rounds and setting up a small roadside shop.

Park Farm now has a tearoom, a farm shop and a garden centre.

"We've worked hard, been lucky in many respects but on the whole it's been brilliant," reflected Margaret.

She said she was proud that so many of her family were still involved in running the farm.

"There's a lot of us - I have six children, 12 grandchildren and 11 great-grandchildren, so it's quite a few. There's always a pram around!"

The farm currently has about 80 cows and sheep.

Its own produce is used in the tearoom and shop.

"Our food miles are really low", said Margaret's daughter-in-law, Margaret Lees Jr.

"We make things in the tearoom from scratch. We use our own milk and cream and we source eggs locally.

"Our customers love the fact that they know where the food is coming from."

The younger Margaret said farmers were facing many challenges, particularly related to new legislation and paperwork.

She said England produced "some of the best beef, lamb and milk in the world" and farming could help provide the country with more food security.

"I think there is a future for the industry but the powers-that-be have to listen to farmers," she said.

title: Trump: Supreme Court tariff, birthright citizenship rulings costing country ‘trillions and trillions of dollars’
description: President Trump on Wednesday claimed the Supreme Court striking down his emergency tariffs and executive order restricting birthright citizenship cost the country “trillions and trillions” of dollars....
fullText:
President Trump on Wednesday claimed the Supreme Court striking down his emergency tariffs and executive order restricting birthright citizenship cost the country "trillions and trillions" of dollars.

Trump wrote on Truth Social, "Does anybody have any idea how much Money and Prestige the United States Supreme Court has cost our Nation with their negative Rulings on Birthright Citizenship and TARIFFS? The answer, TRILLIONS AND TRILLIONS OF DOLLARS!"

The high court overturned the president's emergency tariffs and order on birthright citizenship during its latest term, overruling two key tenets of his economic and immigration agendas.

In February, the justices ruled that Trump did not have the authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to unilaterally impose tariffs on trading partners.

The ruling required the Trump administration to provide restitution to firms that paid higher prices for imported goods, while the president has leaned on different statutes to impose other levies. As of June 29, U.S. Customs and Border Protection had issued roughly $104.29 billion in refunds, according to a court filing.

Last month, the justice also invalidated Trump's order requiring a baby born on U.S. soil to have at least one parent with citizenship or permanent legal status to gain birthright citizenship.

Members of the court's conservative majority sided against the administration each time, with Justice Amy Coney Barrett the lone Trump appointee in the majority of both cases.

While Trump said earlier this month he would ask the court to rehear the birthright citizenship case, the deadline for the Justice Department to petition for a rehearing passed earlier this week. Multiple GOP lawmakers, meanwhile, have introduced legislation to codify the order.

The president has argued that the Supreme Court's ruling will benefit U.S. adversaries, notably Russia and China.

But researchers from Princeton University, Cornell University and Notre Dame University estimated earlier this year that beneficiaries of birthright citizenship contributed $7.7 trillion to the American economy through income from 1975 to 2024.

title: Explosive diarrhea parasite cases rise by thousands, now in 45 states
description: There have been 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases of the explosive diarrhea illness since May 1, the CDC said July 28.
fullText:
Cases of cyclosporiasis, a stomach-churning parasitic infection known for causing explosive diarrhea, have now reached 45 states as infections climb well into the thousands.

There have been 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases of the illness since May 1, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its weekly update on July 28, a more than 2,500 increase since its last report on July 21. Cases have also now been recorded in 45 states, up from 41 last week. More than 11,500 additional cases, primarily in Michigan and Ohio, have not yet been confirmed by laboratories, the CDC said.

There have been 423 hospitalizations and no deaths, per the agency.

Federal health authorities are still investigating the sources of what they believe to be multiple separate outbreaks, the largest of which is centered in Michigan. The state reported more than 10,000 cases of cyclosporiasis on July 29 – numbers which differ from the CDC because they have not yet been officially confirmed and reported back to the federal agency for counting.

This largest outbreak has been linked to iceberg lettuce grown by produce giant Taylor Farms in central Mexico, prompting the company to initiate a recall on July 17.

"Cyclosporiasis cases may not be limited to these states with known cases," according to the CDC update. "The true number of people sick with cyclosporiasis was likely higher than the number reported. This is because some people recover without medical care and are not tested for Cyclospora."

Only Hawaii, Maine, Montana, New Mexico and South Carolina have been spared thus far from the outbreaks. Michigan and Ohio remain the two states most impacted, and Washington, DC, has also reported a handful of cases.

The CDC only reports lab-confirmed cases that occurred on or after May 1 in people who did not travel internationally within 14 days of illness onset. Its numbers often lag behind those cited by state health officials because of tracking, verification and reporting processes. There's typically a six-week reporting lag between an illness and the case being reported to the CDC.

Cyclosporiasis is a parasitic infection that causes unpleasant gastrointestinal symptoms often associated with food poisoning, such as diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. It is caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis, also known simply as cyclospora, and is usually contracted through contaminated food or water.

While unpleasant, it is not generally known to cause death, and many cases go unreported, as people recover at home without visiting a doctor. It can cause more serious complications in people with compromised immune systems or other underlying health issues.

The most common symptom is watery, frequent and sometimes "explosive" diarrhea, according to the CDC and Cleveland Clinic, though other troubles can include:

Bloating, including burping and gas, or stomach cramps.

The Michigan-centered outbreak linked by the Food and Drug Administration to recalled iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms has been identified as the largest nationwide, with the state reporting 10,077 cases as of July 29.

Illnesses from the lettuce outbreak have been confirmed in nine states, including Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, according to the CDC.

These states were identified after health officials tested sick people and traced the "DNA," so to speak, of the infections to determine if they were related. Those that are related are considered part of the same outbreak, likely stemming from the same source. Thus far, these nine states are the only ones the CDC has been able to confirm as related to each other and trace back to the lettuce.

The source of a cyclosporiasis outbreak is more difficult to track than foodborne illnesses because of a long incubation period, difficulty obtaining samples and the inability to use the same genetic tracking tools available for pathogens like E. coli and listeria, as previously reported by USA TODAY.

Several other, separate case clusters have been identified by the CDC and FDA, with no common cause yet named. And while Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a July 21 news briefing that the outbreak was "under control," critics have pointed toward cuts to relevant health agencies, with some saying that scaled-back surveillance and limited staffing enabled not only the cyclospora spread, but other recent outbreaks like screwworm.

Last year, the CDC scaled back a decades-long federal-state partnership that monitors foodborne illnesses, including those caused by cyclospora.

Mexican health authorities, meanwhile, have also said there has not yet been ample evidence to support the FDA's assertion that the outbreak originated over the border, as reported by USA TODAY.]

(This story has been updated to add new information.)

Contributing: Melina Khan, Mike Snider, Sara Moniuszko, USA TODAY; Reuters

title: Ex-Newsom mistress exposes wild affair step by step, reveals Kamala Harris advice to stay quiet
description: Ruby Rippey detailed her affair with then-Mayor Gavin Newsom step-by-step in "Vanity Fair," revealing Kamala Harris privately advised her to stay silent.
fullText:
Ruby Rippey, the woman whose affair with then-Mayor Gavin Newsom sparked a 2007 California political scandal, detailed the encounter step-by-step in a piece published Tuesday in Vanity Fair, while revealing the role former Vice President Kamala Harris played in advising her afterward.

Rippey, who was married to Newsom's campaign manager at the time, Alex Tourk, and who served as the mayor's appointments secretary, disclosed that Harris, who, at the time was the San Francisco District Attorney, privately advised Rippey to "pause" and refrain from public comment or taking a book deal as the scandal broke.

"She listens, then says simply: 'I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective,'" Rippey claims Harris told her after the affair became public.

Kamala Harris Is The 'Fairly Obvious' 2028 Presidential Frontrunner, Democratic Insiders Say

The essay chronicles Rippey's battle with alcoholism, the eventual breakdown in her marriage and her journey to sobriety, while questioning how Newsom's team framed the affair in his memoir.

Rippey notes that Newsom's book wrongly claims he was the one who "came clean" to her husband, a detail she says gives him credit for a confession she had already made. When she asked a Newsom advisor if the governor "tells the truth" in the book, he responded, "Well, we all remember things differently, don't we, Ruby?"

Rippey described beginning the affair while working at City Hall, detailing encounters that included sitting in a hot tub together, spending nights in hotel rooms, and visiting his Russian Hill penthouse.

Newsom Pac Bought Thousands Of Memoir Copies About His Hardships, Juicing Sales

"The next clear memory is getting into the back of my boss's chauffeured town car, heading to The Carneros Inn," Rippey wrote, later adding, "I stretch my legs across the center console and let my heels fall off. He is in the front seat. He takes one of my feet and begins to massage it, the gesture half-hidden inside the loud car."

Rippey described waking up beside Newsom the next morning, noting that while the encounters continued for months, they were fueled by addiction and status: "We meet and we drink. There is sex, but it isn't the point. The point is proximity — to power, to being chosen, to feeling newly visible — no longer muted by pregnancy, by new motherhood, by the strain of white-knuckling long stretches of sobriety."

One comment she claims Newsom made came after the birth of her first child, when they met at a Mexican restaurant. He told her, "Hey — you look really good ... You've lost all your pregnancy weight."

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

Rippey notes that while she entered into the affair willingly, years later she realized the power imbalance may have played a role in the ordeal, adding that "power does not need to coerce. It only needs to exist."

After she decided to come clean to her husband in an email while he was still working for Newsom, Tourk confronted the mayor and immediately resigned. The affair erupted publicly shortly after, prompting Newsom to admit to the affair during a 2007 news conference and subsequently announce he would seek treatment for alcohol abuse.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's team and Harris' team for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax was designed to hit the wealthy, but it’s sending most New Yorkers to their estate lawyers
description: Trusts and LLCs offer not only anonymity from public records, but also a way to protect your assets from liabilities.
fullText:
New York City's pied-à-terre tax was designed to extract money from second-home owners wealthy enough not to live in the city full-time. A side effect no one planned for: it's pushing middle-class and working homeowners, people who already live in their houses, into estate-planning conversations they've never had before, at hourly rates they've never had to pay, for advice the wealthy have had access to for generations.

The rush of publicity accompanying the mayor's office highlighting a list of over 680,000 New York properties that could theoretically be subject to a new tax has inadvertently advertised how public most property data is. And it's advertised the benefits of seeking some totally legal privacy, or risk inadvertent doxxing, courtesy of Gracie Mansion.

"The wealthy and the ultra-high-net-worth have been in this game for a long time," said Myles Fischer, a partner who co-leads the Trusts and Estates practice group at Harris Beach Murtha. "The rest are sort of catching up." And that isn't cheap. Many middle-class and blue-collar homeowners are "being forced into a situation where they have to sit down with lawyers" to get planning advice that families with means secured years ago. After all, he added, "it's not that you have to be a rich person to have something worth protecting. We see it from across the board."

The trigger, in this case, was a public records disclosure. When the DOF released its supplemental pied-à-terre assessment file, the coverage focused on the penthouses and the LLCs holding them. But the unfiltered file swept in far more than luxury properties—it included modest homes in Bayside, single-family houses in Staten Island, properties whose owners may have had no idea their name, address, and assessed value were sitting in a publicly searchable dataset. Many still don't.

Fischer wasn't surprised by the reaction. "Anonymity is desirable when it can be achieved," he said, "but anonymity is also typically only one piece of the pie, so to speak. It's part of the tax plan, part of the estate plan, part of the asset protection, limitation-on-liability sort of pie." Privacy, in other words, is the door. The estate planning is what's behind it.

For Fischer, the most fundamental reason to move real estate into an LLC or trust has nothing to do with taxes or public records. It's liability—the kind that applies to a million-dollar house in Staten Island as directly as it does to a Central Park South penthouse. (The median price to buy a cooperative in Manhattan is $850,000 and to buy a condo it's $1.75 million, netting out to $1.225 million combined.)

title: Ukrainian soldier says the drone-filled 'zero line' is so dangerous that troops sometimes have to wait a week just to move 300 meters
description: At Ukraine's zero line, even tiny movements can be "a question of life and death," so soldiers need to wait long stretches for the right conditions.
fullText:
A Ukrainian soldier said troops may wait a week to move 300 meters at the zero line.

Drones make even small movements a life-or-death calculation, he told BI.

Fog, rain, wind, and electronic warfare can create brief windows to move.

Ukraine's drone-saturated "zero line" is so dangerous that troops may have to wait days for a safe chance to move just a few hundred meters, a Ukrainian soldier told Business Insider.

The soldier, who uses the call sign Yankee, said that he has experienced cases at the zero line, the forward edge of the front line, where "if you want to sometimes move 300 meters, you can't move for seven days."

Moving even that short distance, he said, "can be like a question of life and death." Troops may need favorable weather, electronic-warfare support, and coordination among several Ukrainian units before attempting it.

"You need to make sure you have a cover of radio frequencies. The radio frequencies of the drones are put down," he said.

Doing so can involve Ukrainian electronic-warfare teams detecting and jamming frequencies used by Russian drones, disrupting their operators' ability to control the aircraft or receive video. Such operations require coordination to avoid interfering with Ukraine's own drones.

"The weather is the main component of it. If the weather is not right, you're not going to make it," Yankee said. "So you need either fog, rain, or wind that is 14 meters per second, at least, to do this. So you need to wait for the right conditions."

Fog and rain can obscure drone cameras, while strong winds can make some drones harder to launch and control.

Yankee spoke with Business Insider at Operation Legio, a Norway-led multinational program training and equipping Ukrainian land forces in Poland. He said he was learning NATO standards and tactics to use when he returns to Ukraine.

Yankee serves as a battery sergeant in a front-line unit equipped with man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS. These shoulder-fired missiles can engage drones, missiles, and low-flying aircraft. His unit provides air defense at the zero line and along routes leading to it, he said.

The zero line is the point where Ukrainian soldiers are closest to Russian forces. It is the forwardmost part of the battlefield, where the opposing armies may engage each other directly. Soldiers in this perilous part of the battlefield must remain concealed from enemy troops and the drones searching for them.

The drone and weaponry concentration there is so high that soldiers have described being stuck there for months on end. The movement required to rotate out is highly dangerous.

Drone surveillance is constant, and the enemy is so close that attacks come with little warning. It's an area where soldiers can face both remote drone attacks and close combat with Russian soldiers, including small Russian infiltration groups that regularly approach, trying to find Ukrainian weaknesses. These challenges are tactically and psychologically daunting for troops in the field.

Even areas farther back from the zero line are extremely perilous, with attack and surveillance drones threatening troops and vehicles well behind the forwardmost positions. Ukrainian soldiers and officials describe the front as a "kill zone" that stretches up to 50 kilometers from the zero line on both sides. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a "death zone" where any tank, armored vehicle, or motorcycle that enters it "burns." He said that "everything is destroyed by drones."

Ukrainian troops have said that navigating this deadly area to reach front-line positions can be among the most dangerous parts of a mission. To reduce the chance that a single strike eliminates several people at once, some units have taken to spreading their soldiers farther apart while moving.

Yankee said it was "like Mission Impossible" just to get through this and get to the zero line in the first place.

Ukraine is increasingly trying to use drones and ground robots to conduct operations instead of sending soldiers into the most exposed areas.

But humans are still needed to operate weapons, prepare uncrewed systems, hold forward positions, and perform other tasks that Ukraine has not fully automated. For now, technology can reduce some of the risk at the front line, but it cannot remove soldiers from it.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Mammoth remains revealed in Bulgaria after Danube water levels hit record low
description: SOFIA, July 29 () - The remains of what is believed to be an ancient mammoth ‌have been revealed in northern Bulgaria, after Danube ‌River water levels receded to a record low level, the BTA ​news age...
fullText:
SOFIA, July 29 (Reuters) - The remains of what is believed to be an ancient mammoth ‌have been revealed in northern Bulgaria, after Danube ‌River water levels receded to a record low level, the BTA ​news agency reported on Wednesday, citing historians.

The animal's remains were found on Wednesday by a local resident of the Ryahovo village, who noticed the unusual find ‌on the river bed. ⁠Villagers then alerted specialists in the Regional History Museum in the nearby town of ⁠Ruse.

Museum Director Nikolay Nenov told BTA that experts who were sent to the site recognised a lower ​jaw, two ​tusks and possibly a ​mammoth rib, and that ‌the bones will be removed for further examination on Thursday to establish with accuracy the origin and age of the find.

"I would not call it a sensation, but any discovery of such ancient remains is ‌very important for science," Nenov ​said, adding it has been ​long believed that the ​site was a swamp where the ‌animal probably died thousands of ​years ago.

Danube levels ​have fallen to record lows in recent weeks following the summer's prolonged heat waves and drought ​that have ‌affected rivers across Europe including key waterways such ​as the Rhine.

title: Joe Rogan warns liberals against trying to turn Texas blue, says it would wreck the state's 'delicate balance'
description: Joe Rogan says liberals moving to Texas and voting for far-left policies will destroy the political balance that makes Austin work for everyone.
fullText:
Podcaster Joe Rogan warned liberals Tuesday that moving to Texas and turning the state blue would ruin the delicate balance for everybody, including liberal Texans.

"The liberals that want to turn Texas blue, like, don't. You're going to ruin it," he said.

Rogan, a former Californian, has spoken out numerous times about his choice to leave California over its far-left policies, particularly those from the COVID-19 pandemic years.

Coastal Workers Fleeing Blue Strongholds Could Create An Opportunity For Detroit

Rogan lamented that many "coastal elites" and "coastal snobs" often "have this idea of it being filled with rednecks and ignorant people and foolish people. It's not that way at all. Especially Austin. Austin is like one of the most, like, liberal, easygoing, progressive cities, but even the progressives here, they're like, more reasonable."

He specified that liberal Texans, while they shifted somewhat leftward in recent years, are nowhere near the same far-left positions as those of Los Angeles or New York.

"There's this saying about Austin: 'Keep Austin Weird … and surrounded,'" Rogan said.

"And surrounded? What is the 'and surrounded?'" guest Forrest Galante asked.

"Surrounded by red people. Like it's all red states around you, and it's this pocket of blue that's in the center of this red state," Rogan said. "I think that's good for everybody. I think that's good. It's a balance."

Rogan warned against liberals fleeing blue states only to vote for the same left-wing policies. He compared the state's delicate political balance to that of an ecosystem.

"You're going to ruin it," he warned. "You're going to ruin it for you too. You don't get it. Balance is important. … You can't kill all the predators because then the deer get overrun, and you're hitting them with cars. And you can't kill all the deer because then there's no food. That's what they did when they were market hunting. Balance. And you need balance with humans, too.

"The Austin balance is a great balance," Rogan continued. "It's a liberal city surrounded by, like, hardcore Republicans with guns and tigers."

Joe Rogan Mocks Gavin Newsom For Dismissing Growing State Problems As La Film Production Craters

In 2023, Rogan noted that he got the idea to leave amid the riots in 2020 after the death of Minneapolis resident George Floyd.

"I was like, 'This ain't going in a good direction, and I f---ing smell chaos," he said.

More recently, in 2026, he blasted California Gov. Gavin Newsom for his defense of California, warning instead that Los Angeles may go the way of Detroit as the film industry implodes and companies flee the state.

The latest IRS migration data show Texas is seeing billions of dollars in taxpayer wealth flowing into the state, while Census figures show the state's largest metropolitan areas continue to outpace much of the country in population growth.

Dallas-Fort Worth added more residents than any metropolitan area in the country over the past year, while Houston, Austin and San Antonio also ranked among the nation's fastest-growing metros.

Fox News Digital's Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

title: His son was just sentenced to life without parole for a school shooting. Today, Colin Gray learns his own fate
description: Days after teenage school shooter Colt Gray was sentenced to life in prison, his father is set to appear in the same courtroom for his own sentencing in a landmark case that pushes the limits of who i...
fullText:
Days after teenage school shooter Colt Gray was sentenced to life in prison, his father is set to appear in the same courtroom for his own sentencing in a landmark case that pushes the limits of who is responsible for a mass shooting.

Colin Gray, whose son killed four people at Apalachee High School in 2024, was convicted of murder and manslaughter earlier this year after buying his son an AR-15-style rifle as a Christmas gift and leaving it unsecured – despite warnings his son was a danger to others.

His trial was part of a broader push to hold accountable the parents of juvenile mass shooters. He is the first parent of a school shooter to be convicted of murder.

His sentencing Thursday is part of an emotionally fraught week for the community. Colt pleaded guilty to murder last Friday and was sentenced to life in prison without parole Tuesday. Meanwhile, Apalachee High School's first day of class is this Friday.

Colin Gray's sentencing represents the end of a harrowing road that began with the September 2024 shooting in which his son, then 14, fatally shot two students and two teachers and injured nine others at his Winder, Georgia, high school.

The hearing in Barrow County court is expected to begin with victims' families and survivors, many of whom spoke powerfully at Colt's sentencing. Prosecutors and defense attorneys will then have the chance to debate the length of Colin Gray's prison sentence. He will also have a chance to speak before the judge issues a sentence.

The two second-degree murder charges are each punishable by 10 to 30 years in prison. Under Georgia law, a judge can decide whether a defendant serves that sentence in prison or on probation, so Colin Gray could be released Thursday.

He has already served just under two years since his arrest a day after the shooting.

Colt Gray, now 16, pleaded guilty to 55 felony counts, including four counts of malice murder, on Friday. His three-day sentencing hearing featured emotional victim impact statements, tapes of his confessions to police and insights into his twisted desire for infamy and obsession with school shooters.

The teen declined to speak to the court. He was sentenced Tuesday to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

This case bore close similarities to the trials of James and Jennifer Crumbley, whose then-15-year-old son killed four students in 2021 at his high school in Oxford, Michigan. The Crumbley parents were each convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 10 to 15 years in prison. Their son was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

In a two-week trial in February and March, Barrow County prosecutors argued the boy's father acted with "criminal negligence" and was a proximate cause of the shooting. His defense team, meanwhile, argued he was unaware of his son's violent plans and had taken steps to get him help for his mental health troubles.

The state's case included emotional testimony from students and teachers, police interviews with Colin Gray, photos showing unsecured firearms and ammunition in a bedroom closet, and testimony from the teen's mother, grandmother and sister about Colt's spiraling mental health.

Marcee Gray, the defendant's estranged wife, testified their son was riddled with anxiety, easily agitated and had panic attacks. She said it was "very obvious" he needed professional help, but her husband "just didn't want to deal with it."

Notably, the jury saw body-camera footage from May 21, 2023, when deputies with the Jackson County Sheriff's Office visited Colt and Colin Gray's home after receiving an FBI tip about an online threat to shoot up a school. Colt denied posting the threat, and law enforcement was ultimately not able to substantiate the tip.

Colin Gray bought his son the AR-15-style rifle later that year as a Christmas gift.

The defense called just one witness: Colin Gray himself. He testified he bought his son the firearm and ammunition in an attempt to get him interested in the outdoors and for father-son bonding. He said he had scheduled counseling at school for Colt's mental health issues and did not ever perceive his son as a threat.

"He's a good kid," the father said through tears. "He wasn't perfect, nor was I, but to do something that heinous, I don't know that anybody can see that kind of evil. The Colt I knew, the relationship I had, there was this whole other side of Colt I didn't know existed."

Yet in a tense cross-examination, he acknowledged multiple firearms were stored in a closet, unsecured and unlocked, and he said Colt sometimes kept the rifle in his bedroom. He struggled to explain why Colt did not attend school his entire eighth-grade year, per school records. Colt attended Apalachee High School for only a few days before the attack.

Further, Colin Gray admitted he was aware that his son had been physically violent, had a photo of a school shooter on his bedroom wall and had texted a few weeks before the attack, "Whenever something happens, just know the blood is on your hands."

The jury deliberated for less than two hours and convicted him of all 27 charges: Two counts of second-degree murder, two counts of involuntary manslaughter, 18 counts of cruelty to children and five counts of reckless conduct.

Marcee Gray, the teen's mother, was not charged in the case. She had lost custody of Colt because of her struggles with drugs and alcohol and did not possess the firearms, Barrow County District Attorney Brad Smith said.

"We found what she did to be morally reprehensible. We do not believe she is a good mother, in my opinion," he said. "But at the end of the day, she did not have custody of Colt, she did not have proximity to Colt, and she was not the one that provided him the firearms."

Colin Gray's trial also revealed the shooting was nearly prevented. The morning of the shooting, school officials and resource officers went to intercept Colt Gray after he had made several concerning comments. But in a stranger-than-fiction mix-up, they confused him with another student named Kolton Gray.

Colt Gray then armed himself with the AR-15-style rifle – which he had hidden in his backpack – and fired indiscriminately into a math class and shot several people in the hallway.

Teachers Richard Aspinwall and Cristina Irimie and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo were killed.

CNN's Devon Sayers, Isabel Rosales and Maxime Tamsett contributed to this report.

title: Five Hacks Every Boox Palma User Should Know
description: Get the most out of your phone-shaped e-reader.
fullText:
While the Kindle is the most popular e-reader in the world, it's not the best option for people who want more control over their digital libraries. If you're a true e-book nerd, you've probably heard of the Boox Palma, the e-ink device with a phone-like form factor that has attracted a huge cult following on social media.

The thing about the Palma, though, is that it's way more than an e-reader—it costs about the same as an Android tablet because it basically is one. You can sideload your e-books to read on the native reading app (called NeoReader), or you can install most any app from the Google Play Store. In short, it can do way more than a Kindle, but that also means it can be way more complicated to get it working how you want to. To that end, here are five ways to get more out of your Boox e-reader (whether that's the original Palma, the Palma 2, or the Palma 2 Pro).

Unlike all modern Kindles, the Boox Palma still has physical buttons, which is a big plus for anyone who prefers not to turn pages with a touchscreen. Unfortunately, not all apps are configured to recognize a press of the volume up or down button as a request to turn the page. Fortunately, this is typically an easy fix, though you'll have to check your settings in a few different spots to get it working.

To use the volume buttons to turn pages in the Kindle app: Because Kindle is the most popular reading app, bespoke instructions are in order—especially because they are hardly intuitive.

Open the Kindle app and navigate to any book.

Tap the center of the screen to bring up the reading overlay menu, then tap the "Aa" icon to open display settings.

Tap the "Layout" tab and make sure the slider next to "Continuous Scrolling" is turned off.

Now tap the "More" tab and scroll down until you see "Turn Pages with Volume Controls" and set that slider to on.

While specific instructions might be different depending on your reading app of choice, there's also a system-level settings option you can try to enable page turns with the volume buttons:

Long-press the app icon on the home screen to open quick settings and tap "Optimize."

Next to the "Customize Buttons" menu option you'll see three icons; tap the one on the far left that looks like in a circle to set the Volume button setting to "Page-turning." (Incidentally, if you prefer to use the volume buttons to trigger the continuous scroll option, that's what the up/down arrow icon on the right is for).

If you're a "turn pages with the buttons" kind of person, you might also want to turn off the touchscreen so you don't accidentally turn the page if you touch the screen accidentally or put your Palma in your pocket without putting it to sleep first. Unfortunately, there's no system- or app-level setting for this, but you can accomplish it with a third-party app.

There are a ton of options for these kinds of apps on the Google Play Store, but some of them will go too far by disabling physical buttons as well, while others will fill your screen with ads. A better alternative is an app called Touch Protector, but it's not on Google Play—so you'll have to install the Aptoide app store first. Aptoide is a decentralized, open-source alternative to Google Play.

Note: Using a decentralized app store means you're opening yourself up to a bit more risk, so look for apps with the green "Trusted" icon, indicating that they have been scanned for malware and compared against apps in other app stores to ensure they aren't copycats. You'll also need to be comfortable with overriding some system-level security recommendations; I wouldn't do this on a device I use for financial transactions or reading e-mails, but all I do with my Palma is read. In short, go with your gut on this one.

With those disclaimers out of the way, here are the steps involved:

Navigate to the Aptoide app store from your Palma's web browser, then tap the "More" option on the lower right; on the next screen, tap "Get Aptoide." (You'll have to click through some permissions screens indicating you understand there's risk in downloading an app APK file from an "unknown" source.)

Once you've downloaded the Aptoide APK file, open it from your downloads folder and install it (this will require another security acknowledgement).

Once installed, open Aptoide and search for "Touch Protector" (or use this link). The first time you use Aptoide, you'll be prompted to give it system-level permission to install apps; it will open the relevant settings menu automatically. (If you have a Boox Palma 2 Pro running Android 15, you may also receive a message indicating that Touch Protector was designed for an earlier version of Android, but you can choose to install it anyway.)

Open the Touch Protector app. The first time you do, you'll be prompted to give it "Display over other apps" permissions. The settings menu for this option will likewise open automatically; scroll down to Touch Protector, tap it, and turn the slider to "On." (If Android prevents you from doing this here, you'll need to do it manually: Open Settings > Apps & Notifications > Applications. Find "Touch Protector" in the apps list and tap the slider next to "Display on top of other apps.")

Now you'll need to configure your Touch Protector settings to choose how you'll lock and unlock the touchscreen. I suggest tapping "Shake," which allows you to toggle the option on or off by gently shaking your device. (Yes, you can adjust how hard you need to shake it so you won't do so accidentally.)

All of that accomplished, you can now temporarily disable the touchscreen in whatever reading app you're using by shaking your Palma. Shake it again when you want touch controls back.

Like any e-ink tablet, Boox devices suffer from occasional "ghosting," or visible afterimages once you've turned a page. While the device will automatically refresh itself after a certain number of screen touches and you can adjust your settings so it refreshes more often, I like to set a one-touch refresh that I can trigger whenever I want. This is convenient, because some types of content, including anything with images, will require more frequent refreshes than others. There are two ways to set a one-touch manual refresh: a button or a gesture.

Use a button to perform a one-touch refresh: Though you could map this function to any button, it makes most sense to use the Palma's Smart Button for this—that's the button on the top left-hand side of the device, and it can do different things based on whether you press it once, twice, or hold it down. On my own Palma, I've mapped a manual refresh to a single Smart Button press, as it's the thing I find myself doing most often (a long-press takes me back to the home screen). To remap your Smart Button, open the Settings app and tap "Smart Button." Tap your preferred option ("Short-press Function," "Double-click Function," or "Long-press Function") and select "Full-refresh."

Use a gesture to perform a one-touch refresh: Open Settings and scroll down to "System Navigation." Under "Bottom Navigation," tap "More Settings." Choose the area of the screen you'd like to map the refresh to by swiping between the left, center, or right side options. Tap "Custom" and then choose "Full-refresh" from your list of options.

Listening to audiobooks or podcasts on the Palma can be a frustrating experience, especially if you have a case with a magnetic cover that puts the device to sleep when you close it, as doing so will also pause any audio you're listening to. However, you can fix this with a few settings changes.

The first thing you'll need to do is adjust your settings to allow apps that play audio to continue running in the background. In the interest of preserving battery life, the Palma OS turns this setting off for every app you download from the Google Play Store, but you can change that. First, you can long-press the icon of any app on the home screen. This will bring up a menu with a few different options. Tap "Optimize." From the next pop-up menu, select the "Others" tab, then make sure the slider next to "Stay active in the background" is turned to On.

Next, you need to "unfreeze" background apps so they don't try to update when not in use. You can make this change globally, or on a per-app basis. Freezing apps improves battery life, so keep that in mind as you make your decision. To unfreeze a single app, open Settings and scroll down to "Apps and Notifications." Tap "Freeze Settings," find your audio-playing apps in the list of installed programs, and turn the slider to off. To unfreeze all your apps, from this same menu, turn the "Do not freeze apps running in the background (audio, input methods, etc.)" slider to On.

The last thing you'll need to do is keep the Palma from turning off Bluetooth and disconnecting your headphones after the device goes to sleep. To do that, open Settings and scroll to Power. On the next screen, tap "Bluetooth Status After Sleep" and select "Stay Connected" from the pop-up menu. (I'd also suggest turning on "Always turn Bluetooth on when the device starts up" from this menu, so you won't have to manually turn Bluetooth on every time you want to connect your headphones—though this too will affect your overall battery life).

You might assume that because your Palma is signed in to Google Play and active in your account, locating it (or triggering lost mode) will work—but you also need to have location services turned on at the system level, or you'll be out of luck. To do this, go to Settings and scroll down to "Location Information." Turn on the slider next to "Access my location information." You can then tap "Location permission of apps" to adjust the settings for any apps you don't want tracking you, while still keeping your pricey e-reader perfectly findable.

Note that in order to be findable, your device must be turned on and connected to the internet. For the Palma 2, that means whoever finds it will need to turn it on and connect it to wifi; for the Palma 2 Pro with an active SIM card, it will likewise need to be powered on and not in sleep mode.

title: Nano Banana 2 Is Coming to Google Earth
description: You can now use Nano Banana 2 on Google Earth on the web to imagine historical scenes and futuristic developments.
fullText:
Known by the codename Nano Banana 2, the most recent AI image generation updates added to Google Gemini have been a significant step forward in terms of quality and accuracy, and now similar capabilities are being plugged into the Google Earth app on the web. It means you're able to use the aerial, satellite, and 3D imagery packed into Google Earth as the basis for prompts for AI images—maybe peering into the distant past with a historical reconstruction or looking to the future with a sci-fi reimagining.

We've already seen just how precise and realistic the Nano Banana-powered features in Google Gemini are now, and Google has five suggestions for how you might deploy these capabilities in Google Earth. First, you can learn while exploring, so maybe getting the AI to build an infographic on the Statue of Liberty with key historical facts about it.

A text prompt such as "reimagine this empty lot in Tokyo as a vibrant shopping and retail district with open spaces" would transform a rather bare part of the Google Earth 3D map into something quite different. You can also visualize personal projects such as a dream lakeside home or an extension for your current property. Google Earth would combine the existing landscape with whatever you prompted, and help you come up with ideas as part of the planning stage.

You can also look forwards and backwards. "Sometimes it’s fun to let your imagination run wild," says Google, suggesting that you might want to get the AI to imagine how a place might look in a hundred years. (It might be worth nudging your prompt towards a utopian rather than dystopian vision of the future.)

Finally, Google suggests you dive back into the past. The company showcased a demo with the prompt "render a hyper-realistic view of what these Pompeii ruins looked like in 78 AD," which could be used by teachers, for example. That would instantly transform today's ruins "into a bustling, colorful street scene from the Roman Empire," in Google's words.

These new features come with the usual AI image caveats, however. While Nano Banana 2 can pull real-world information and images from the web, and is able to render graphics with more consistency and accuracy than previous models, there's still going to be the usual weaknesses involved with AI: Your lakeside home might not be entirely structurally sound, and the Pompeii reconstruction may not be entirely authentic—so bear that in mind when your images are produced.

When I asked Google about this, a representative emphasized the real-world knowledge base that Nano Banana 2 draws on, which includes all the text and graphics it can find online, as well as the vast number of images that have been plugged into the AI during its training. With Google Earth, it will also trace over the structure ruins that are still in place when it comes to Pompeii, for example.

For a bit more clarity, you can try quizzing the Nano Banana 2 model inside the main Gemini app: I got it to render an imagined scene from Pompeii just prior to it being smothered by Vesuvius, then asked about the image accuracy. The AI said it had combined a bunch of real, historical information points to render the scene, including details on Pompeii's raised sidewalks, and the clothing styles of the day. Google hasn't said anything specific about usage limits, but the Nano Banana 2 upgrade is rolling out now globally, for all users of Google Earth on the web.

title: A bolt from the blue as Welsh boxers go for gold
description: Rosie Eccles, Owain Harris-Allan, Orlando Holley-Sotomi join super heavyweight Connor Williams in guaranteeing themselves a Commonwealth Games medal.
fullText:
In the opening minute of his quarter-final bout, Orlando Holley-Sotomi caught his opponent with a couple of straight right hands.

At 68 seconds, he unleashed another.

The thunderous shot, followed by a left hook, sent Lesotho's Refiloe Thai to the canvas.

"Watching tape of my opponent, he was open to my backhand," the Newport boxer said.

"My backhand is one of my best shots so I didn't hesitate, I just used it."

Knockouts of this brutality are rare in amateur boxing. 'The General' looked every bit the pro.

After a tense silence when doctors rushed to his aid, Thai got to his feet to relieved applause from the gallery.

When the referee lifted Orlando's dangerous right hand in victory, it marked the end of a successful hour in Glasgow for Welsh boxing on Wednesday afternoon.

Defending champion Rosie Eccles stopped Samukelisiwe Sinothile Ncube in the second round of the women's 70kg before delaying her media duties to watch Owain Harris-Allan win unanimously on points against home favourite Nick Devlin.

Eccles, Harris-Allan and Holley-Sotomi join super heavyweight Connor Williams in guaranteeing themselves a Commonwealth Games medal. In boxing, losing semi-finalists are awarded bronze medals.

So Friday, 30 July will see them seek to upgrade their medal colours ahead of finals the following day.

Here are the four boxers chasing gold for Wales.

The Olympian's glittering CV already includes gold and silver Commonwealth medals but she wants the trilogy'.

The Caldicot light-middleweight, who turned 30 on the day she carried the Welsh flag at the opening ceremony in Glasgow, claims to have "more fire than ever" as she aims to repeat her gold medal in Birmingham.

After revealing she will hang up her gloves after these Games, Eccles says she is trying to keep a lid on her emotions.

"It was an amazing feeling stood waiting to walk out because the journey here has been probably one of my hardest in my career," she said.

"I've had to keep my performance head on and keep the emotion side of it in the box. I could be very emotional and sentimental, but it's one fight at a time.

"We've done some work to get here and I've just got to go and execute now and hopefully make them all proud."

Eccles fights India's Arundhati Choudhary at 15:00 BST for a place in the gold medal bout.

Harris-Allan first entered the ring aged seven to "burn off some energy".

He was 18 in Birmingham when he "snuck through the back door" to claim a bronze medal in Birmingham 2022.

Two years later he narrowly missed out on qualification to box for Team GB at the Paris Olympics.

The Cardiff fighter has talked a big game in the run up to these Games and even cupped his ear to the home crowd after beating Scotland's Nick Devlin in men's lightweight quarter-final.

"They were all loud when he was coming in," he said. "They weren't so loud when I came out.

"I'm not satisfied. I've come for a gold medal and I'll be sure to do that."

Harris-Allan fights India's Sachin Sachin at 20:30 BST.

Holley-Sotomi was a promising rugby player when he first began boxing at 15 years old.

He was in the Dragons academy and picked up the sport in order to improve his fitness.

A three-time Welsh champion, his statement knockout win on Wednesday sets up a semi-final against Mauritius' Merven Clair at 16:00 BST on Friday.

"I've made it to a semi-final before in a major competition at Europeans and I just missed the final," he said.

"So this is a big one for me. I want to get to the finals, avenge myself and just prove that I belong.

"I'm going to make it to a final and I'm going to get a gold medal."

The Swansea boxer has made a rapid rise since joining Welsh boxing's elite programme only last year.

He says his baby boy Cass, named after the great Muhammad Ali, would probably try to eat his medal, whichever colour that may be come Saturday.

"I'm very confident going into the semi-finals," he said.

"I've had two good wins now. I'm building a lot of momentum and I feel like I'm destined for this."

Williams faces Northern Ireland's Garyn McAllister at 16:30 BST on Friday.

Team Wales won six medals at Birmingham 2022 including gold medals for Eccles and Ioan Croft, silver for Taylor Bevan and bronze for Jake Dodd, Harris-Allan and Garan Croft.

Though Wales cannot match that tally in Glasgow, Games success is measured on the number of golds won.

So can the class of 2026 surpass Wales' tally of four years ago?

title: Scottish Rugby sacks chief executive Williamson after inquiry
description: Scottish Rugby sacks its chief executive, Alex Williamson, after a months-long examination of his conduct in the role.
fullText:
Scottish Rugby has sacked its chief executive, Alex Williamson, after a months-long examination of his conduct in the role.

Appointed as successor to Mark Dodson in September 2024, Williamson started work at Murrayfield in early 2025.

A low-key figure, it was announced in late-May this year that he had been put on a period of extended leave. No explanation was offered as to the reason why.

Now John McGuigan, chairman of Scottish Rugby Limited, has announced: "The board of Scottish Rugby has today dismissed Alex Williamson from his position as chief executive with immediate effect.

"His dismissal follows the conclusion of an independent investigation into matters that were brought to the board's attention earlier this year.

"In light of the investigation findings, the board of Scottish Rugby concluded that the CEO's conduct had fallen significantly below the standards we set as an organisation."

Current chief financial officer David White is set to become interim chief executive while the governing body begins the process of replacing Williamson.

Room for improvement but Scotland heading in right direction

Williamson's dismissal came after an extensive inquiry and is hugely embarrassing for Scottish Rugby.

Williamson was appointed after Scottish Rugby failed in a bid to land Mark Darbon as Dodson's replacement.

The deal to sign Darbon, previously chief executive of Northampton Saints in England's Premiership, was almost done, but at a late stage, and to the fury of all at Murrayfield, he took up the position of chief executive at the R&A in St Andrews.

Dodson's exit was a bruising affair for the organisation and Darbon's apparent u-turn was the source of much frustration.

Now they have been cast into another recruitment process.

The next 14 months are enormously important to the SRU, with Nations Championship games at Murrayfield in the autumn - including one against the All Blacks - followed by the Six Nations in the spring and the World Cup beginning in Australia next October.

Williamson's arrival was hailed by Scottish Rugby after his previous roles running the Goodwood Estate and as chief executive of House of Fraser.

"He has a proven track record of achieving commercial growth, accelerating the transformation of established businesses to achieve improved performance and, at the same time, consistently emphasising the importance of authenticity, openness and community values," Scottish Rugby's statement said when announcing his appointment.

Williamson had spoken about the pleasure he would derive from "shaping the future of something that is about so much more than rugby. A sport that brings families together, inspires fans and connects communities in the way Scottish rugby does makes it more important than ever."

At a time when on-field matters seem to be improving - Scotland had an encouraging Six Nations and summer series - uncertainty at the top has returned.
