title: How Tottenham's transfer window shows big WSL ambitions
description: It is clear from Tottenham's summer transfer business that they have big ambitions in the Women's Super League next season.
fullText:
It is clear from Tottenham's summer transfer business that they have big ambitions in the Women's Super League next season.

Martin Ho's side have strengthened in the market, building a squad that, on paper, could cause a stir among the league's top clubs.

They finished fifth in the WSL last season - a significant improvement on the year before when they flirted with relegation.

Tottenham broke their club-record signing this summer to bring in France defender Alice Sombath from Lyon, having spent around £375,000 on Signe Gaupset in January.

They also signed forwards Shekiera Martinez and Kirsty Hanson, defender Caitlin Dijkstra, midfielder Victoria Pelova and goalkeeper Selma Panengstuen.

So how have they approached their transfer business and what are the club's ambitions this year?

It is Spurs' seventh season in the top flight and their growth has been vast - the number of staff has increased and training facilities have improved.

They have their own base at the club's training centre on Hotspur Way but plans for a new women and girls academy facility was blocked in court this week.

Just months after promotion in 2019, they hosted almost 40,000 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium for the north London derby defeat by Arsenal.

A year later, they signed USA superstar Alex Morgan on a short-term loan after she gave birth and in 2024 they reached the Women's FA Cup final.

A disappointing season under Robert Vilahamn in 2024-25 led to his sacking and Ho's subsequent arrival, and Spurs jumped back up the table in his debut campaign.

Since Ho joined the club in July 2025, Tottenham have had a 12-month plan for recruitment and had identified targets in the three windows that followed.

Talks with striker Cathinka Tandberg and defender Toko Koga, who both joined in 2025, were advanced before Ho's contract was finalised and they have become key players under him.

Ho took time to look at the squad in his first summer to see what was needed before implementing widespread evolution plans.

Since then, sources at Tottenham say they signed all of their key targets in January and have already done the same this summer despite the window remaining open until 3 September.

There was a deliberate attempt to get deals wrapped up early so Ho could work with the entire squad for a full pre-season programme.

Meanwhile, managing director Andy Rogers, who has been at Spurs for 24 years, has led their transfer business this summer, keen to leave the club in a strong position and ensure a smooth handover before he steps down.

What that forward-planning and successful business does for Tottenham will be clearer at the end of the season.

They have consolidated their position as a WSL club and have enough off-field resources to start building towards European football.

Ho has been consistent in his messaging, stressing Tottenham's ambition is to compete with the WSL's best and to build a squad capable of playing in Europe.

With only the top three teams in the WSL qualifying for the Women's Champions League and with Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City and Manchester United dominating those spots, it is a huge step for Tottenham to make.

They also have to compete with fellow big-spenders London City Lionesses and Brighton, who themselves have ambitions of breaking into the top three.

Their investment and growth has been a catalyst for Spurs, who know they cannot be left behind in a period when transfer fee records are constantly being broken.

It is also a period in the women's game's development when discussions involving financial regulations and salary caps are still in their infancy.

That means clubs have the ability to pour in more money should they wish and with little regulatory fightback - though that could change in the near future.

Tottenham's spending on the women's side this summer has coincided with an ambitious window for the men's team, who are looking to bounce back from a poor campaign that almost led to their relegation from the Premier League.

It is part of an overall change in strategy following the departure of chairman Daniel Levy in September 2025 and subsequent movement in the boardroom.

Vinai Venkatesham also joined as chief executive officer from Arsenal in April 2025 and was crucial in their women's team's success, something he hopes to emulate at Tottenham.

Another huge challenge for the club remains the growth of the fanbase. Spurs had an average attendance of just 1,734 in the WSL last season - a figure that factored in higher-attended crowds at sporadic matches at the main stadium.

title: Norrie beats Duckworth to reach Los Cabos quarters
description: Cameron Norrie books his place in the Los Cabos Open quarter-finals with a straight-set victory over James Duckworth in Mexico.
fullText:
Cameron Norrie booked his place in the Los Cabos Open quarter-finals with a straight-set victory over James Duckworth in Mexico.

The British number two defeated Australia's Duckworth 6-4 6-4 to set up a meeting with former top-20 player Bernard Tomic in the last eight.

Norrie, who ended a six-match losing streak with a first-round win over Aleksandar Kovacevic, had to fight back from 3-0 down to claim the first set against Duckworth.

He broke twice in the second set to go 5-2 up, and survived a late wobble to serve out victory.

The fifth seed is the second-highest ranked player still in the draw after top seed Jiri Lehecka lost to Hong Kong's Coleman Wong, and Tomic stunned fourth seed Karen Khachanov.

Meanwhile, Naomi Osaka continued her strong form by advancing past Ashlyn Krueger to the quarter-finals of the Washington Open.

Third seed Osaka - who was playing for the first time since reaching the Wimbledon quarter-finals - dominated the match to lead 6-3 3-1 victory over before Krueger retired because of an ankle injury.

Osaka will face Italy's Elisabetta Cocciaretto in her third successive quarter-final.

In the men's singles event, 17-year-old Cruz Hewitt will reunite with top seed Alex de Minaur in the last 16.

Hewitt is the son of former world number one Lleyton Hewitt, and used to knockabout with De Minaur, 10 years his senior.

He defeated Marcos Giron of the United States 6-3 6-4 on his main singles draw debut, while De Minaur beat Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-4 3-6 6-4.

Former world number four Jack Draper withdrew late from Washington because of discomfort in his left arm, but has been awarded a wildcard into the Canadian Open.

Novak Djokovic withdrew from the tournament in Montreal but will enter the Cincinnati Masters next month.

title: Cricket & archery well placed for Commonwealths spot
description: Cricket, archery and shooting are among the sports well placed to regain their spot at the Commonwealth Games in India in 2030.
fullText:
Cricket, archery and shooting are among the sports well placed to regain their spot at the Commonwealth Games in India in 2030.

Only 10 sports were included in the ongoing Glasgow Games because of the rushed build-up after the Australian state of Victoria pulled out as hosts.

Discussions on the sporting programme remain ongoing between Commonwealth Sport, sporting federations and the Indian organising committee for the next Games, which will be held in Ahmedabad, Gujarat.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Commonwealth Sport chief executive Katie Sadlier would not be drawn on the process but India Olympic Association's Raghu Iyer said: "There are many sports who will feel they have missed out.

"There are sports in which India has done very well, shooting, archery and many other sports."

Pushed on whether that puts cricket, which was included for Birmingham 2022 for the first time in 24 years as a women's-only T20 event, archery and shooting at the top of the queue, Iyer added: "While I do not have the mandate to talk about any of these, you have been pretty interesting with the choices you have mentioned…"

"We also want to have sports that India have traditionally done well in," he said.

Boxer Abdul - grandson of dictator - disqualified for headbutt

Cricket's cause is helped by the fact at least two team sports will be added for 2030. Hockey and rugby sevens would be other options.

Badminton, 3x3 basketball and 3x3 wheelchair basketball, beach volleyball, cycling, diving, judo, rhythmic gymnastics, squash, triathlon and para triathlon and wrestling are other sports under consideration.

India can also propose two new sports as host nation and push others that have significance at home. No final decisions have been made.

Ahmedabad will be the Commonwealth's centenary Games and events will held in the 120,000-seater Narendra Modi Stadium, which has hosted two cricket World Cup finals in recent years.

India has also expressed a keen interest in hosting the 2036 Olympic Games, with this potentially a key step in the road.

"Any sporting event will be a step towards that," Iyer said. "We are looking purely at ensuring that these Commonwealth Games are one of the best that have been held."

The reduced programme in Glasgow has helped slash the cost of hosting the Games from around £800m to £160m.

Organisers have been keen to claim this repurposed structure will be cheaper and more appealing for future hosts, but the sporting programme will rise to 17 in Ahmedabad.

"17 is, we think, the right number," Sadlier said.

"The Victoria Games was 26 sports. We recognised we needed to reset and bring the Games into something that was affordable around the Commonwealth.

"What we have done here has been brilliant but we will bring back a few sports. We won't go beyond that number."

Sadlier also rejected concerns around the cut through of the Glasgow Games, given there has been no live television coverage on a major channel in the UK.

"We have got more broadcast deals signed for this Games than we ever have," she said.

"Globally, the reach has been exceptional. On socials we broke the targets from Birmingham last week. It has been an amazingly covered Games."

title: London City host Man Utd to kick off WSL season
description: London City Lionesses are handed a Women's Super League opener against Manchester United as the Women's Super League fixtures are announced.
fullText:
Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas is set to make her London City Lionesses' debut against Manchester United when the Women's Super League season kicks off.

London City will host United in the opening match of the 2026-27 WSL season on Friday, 4 September (19:00 BST).

Spain midfielder Putellas is the highest profile of the eight signings made by Eder Maestre.

His ambitious side face a United team hoping to bounce back after failing to qualify for the Champions League last season.

The BBC will broadcast 25 matches during the campaign, beginning with eight-time champions Chelsea taking on Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, 5 September (12:30 BST), live on BBC One.

The Blues will play all of their home league matches at the main stadium this year, ending a nine-year stay at Kingsmeadow.

On the season's first Sunday, defending champions Manchester City begin their campaign at home against promoted Birmingham City while Tottenham host West Ham United.

Charlton Athletic and Crystal Palace, also promoted from the WSL 2 as the English top flight expands to 14 teams, will host Liverpool and Everton respectively.

Finally, title hopefuls Arsenal return to Brighton where a 1-1 draw in May ensured Manchester City won the 2025-26 Women's Super League.

Full list of 2026-27 Women's Super League fixtures

Man City crowned WSL champions after Arsenal held at Brighton

What's working - and what's not - for WSL fans?

Last season's top three will all face each other before the end of November.

Chelsea host Arsenal on 27 September with the Gunners travelling to Etihad Stadium to play Manchester City a week later on 4 October.

Andree Jeglertz's side are scheduled to go to Stamford Bridge on 14 November, a game that will be live on the BBC.

Also on the BBC will be Manchester United's derby games against Liverpool and Manchester City (currently 4 and 25 October respectively).

Last season, most WSL matches took place at 12:00 on Sundays, a time that was not universally popular given its clash with grassroots fixtures.

For 2026-27, the schedule is more varied, with more games planned for Friday evenings, as well as Saturday lunchtime fixtures and matches staggered across Sunday afternoons, including the return of an evening fixture on certain weeks.

On Tuesday, the WSL released details of its new Players Cup, formerly the League Cup, and the BBC will show March's final in full, as well as numerous matches from the Women's Champions League - including the final - throughout the season.

The campaign will culminate with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil and the BBC will bring extensive coverage of the game's biggest event.

All eyes will be on Putellas' debut in the WSL - and London City have hit the jackpot with a home opener against a United team many believe they can topple this season.

They will want to capitalise on that opportunity to bring in supporters and grow the fanbase - with Putellas, among other star signings including ex-Manchester United goalkeeper Mary Earps, set to be the face of that opening fixture.

It is a tough start for United, who take on London City, Chelsea and Arsenal in their first three games - a run that could show whether they can challenge for the title or are in shape to secure a Champions League spot.

In contrast, champions Manchester City will be pleased with their start, avoiding their closest rivals until October, meaning they could have the chance to open up a lead at the top.

Newcomers Charlton Athletic will play their first ever WSL fixture at home, which is sure to be a great occasion for the club.

The match between Birmingham City and Crystal Palace in September – last season's WSL 2 top two – could be another key one in the calendar.

The big derby matches taking place in February and March always carry intriguing storylines, while the expansion of the league means there is an additional game for fans to watch each weekend.

Naturally, when European competition kicks in, there is scope for the calendar to shuffle around a little but clubs now have an idea of where their tricky spells could occur this season.

title: Scotland & England face losing Para-race medals
description: Melanie Woods faces losing her Commonwealth Games women’s 1500m T54 title after it is decide to stage the race again following an appeal.
fullText:
Scottish Para-athlete Melanie Woods faces losing her Commonwealth Games women’s 1500m T54 gold medal - and her Games record - after it was decided to stage the race again following an appeal.

Woods, 31, set a new mark in streaking to victory in her home city on Wednesday, but the event at Scotstoun was marred by a first-lap crash.

Canada’s Nandini Sharma crossed the line in second place behind Woods, but was disqualified at the time for her role in the incident.

The Canadians‘ appeal against that decision failed and, after further protests by Australia and Mauritius, the Para-athletics authorities - rather than Glasgow 2026 organisers - have ruled that the event should be restaged on Friday.

Woods took gold ahead of England's Ellis Kottas and Mikaela Dingley of Australia, but the ceremony was not due to be held until Thursday, so none of the athletes were actually presented with medals.

The Scot - who was consigned to a chair after being hit by a car while riding her bike in 2018 - is also due to compete in the 400m event in Friday's morning session.

The heats of that will start a little more than 90 minutes after the replayed final.

"We note the decision of the Jury of Appeal regarding the Women's T54 1500m final," Team Scotland said in a statement. "Melanie Woods and Joanna Robertson will now prepare to compete again on Friday in the rerun."

title: The phone call that made Briton an NFL trailblazer
description: Seydou Traore is the first graduate of the UK-based NFL Academy to be drafted in the NFL. This is how he beat the odds.
fullText:
Seydou Traore has been waiting four hours for the phone call that will change his life. When it comes, he is the picture of calm. Next to him, his mum Zaia is anything but.

Traore and his family are sitting backstage at the NFL Draft, where the 23-year-old Briton - who did not see his loved ones for five years after moving to the US to try to become an NFL player - has just been told his dream is coming true.

Zaia, who is French-Algerian, lets out a 'zaghrouta' - a celebratory trilling sound that is traditional in north Africa - sheds tears of joy and has an out-of-body experience in a reaction that goes viral.

"I was in a trance," she tells BBC Sport. "I was like 'oh my God, it's happening, he's done it'. That's what I kept telling myself. It was pride and relief because it's been years, and it was all worth it."

Of all the social media content around Seydou's achievement in being the first graduate of England's NFL Academy to complete his pathway to the NFL, it is the clip of his mum he keeps watching.

He knows that she knows exactly what it has taken to defy the odds and become an NFL trailblazer.

A pep talk from the great Travis Kelce was just a tiny part.

Born and raised in south London, Traore was naturally athletic and tried many sports. He was playing football as a goalkeeper when he found American football at 16 with London Warriors.

In 2019 he earned a place in the first intake at the NFL Academy, a development programme initially based in north London and now in Loughborough. The academy recruits from many sport backgrounds and American football experience is not necessary.

Almost all draft prospects come through the American college system, which is why the academy was designed to help international players earn scholarships and prepare them for the NFL, mentally and physically.

Each year about one million teenagers play American football at high school in the US. About 0.08% of them reach the NFL.

One can therefore imagine how the odds are stacked against an international player like Traore.

But he applied himself to his dream, getting up at 5am and working all day every day to get better, either at the academy or training.

And the following summer, he had a breakthrough.

Traore's mum was in the kitchen when he came in and told her: "Some Americans want to speak with you. I've been talking to them for a while and, basically, I'm going to America."

Unknown to Zaia, her son had secured a spot at Florida high school Clearwater Academy. She told him: "I can't afford to come and see you, you'll be there by yourself."

For Traore's sister Zeinab, four years his senior, the thought of him moving 4,500 miles from home was even more difficult.

"He's like my first child so I'm protective," she says. "I was concerned at first. I thought it was too big a jump because he was still young."

Traore had been laying the foundations for this move for some time, making videos to showcase his skills.

One of them found its way to Clearwater head coach Jesse Chinchar.

"Wow, who's that?" Chinchar wondered as he watched a 6ft 3in guy leaping in the air to make a one-handed catch.

Little did he know that he was watching a Londoner who was yet to play a full-sided game of American football. But Clearwater had a track record of recruiting international players and helping them earn college scholarships.

"I did a bit more digging but there was no game film, just clips of him doing athletic stuff," says Chinchar.

"We got talking to Seydou and it felt like he was going to compete and wanted it for all the right reasons. You could tell how much it meant to him.

"It was kind of a wild adventure because he was one of the most raw, unknown commodities we had brought in, but we thought 'if this kid comes over and it works out, this could change his life'."

From day one Chinchar thought "we got something".

Traore learned his first playbook in a matter of days, which is like learning a new language. And playing as a wide receiver, he was immediately dominant against kids who had played the game their whole life.

He thinks his goalkeeping skills helped.

"Hand-eye coordination, tracking and locating balls, leaping down low or up high, and attacking the ball at corner kicks, that translates very well," Traore says.

"That's how American football is when they throw the ball up to you, you attack it at its highest point."

Chinchar agrees, adding: "I've felt that my guys who had a background in soccer have that understanding of spatial awareness, which I think in [American] football is an under-rated trait."

Chinchar was also impressed by Traore's character and self-belief. Even when he received his first college offer, he bet on himself getting a better one. That eventually came from Arkansas State.

Their head coach Butch Jones was working late when his tight ends coach came into his office and said: "I keep hearing about this player. I think he's special, there's something different about him."

They watched videos of Traore and Jones soon made a "hefty comparison". He called Seydou a clone of Travis Kelce, whom he coached at Cincinnati and helped convert into one of the best tight ends in NFL history.

"Seydou's size and stature coupled with his athleticism - the way he ran, the way he caught the ball – it made him a rare commodity," says Jones. "He had unlimited potential."

Traore had barely played at tight end and had already committed to another college. Jones therefore had to 'flip' him - so he called on his old friend.

He set up a group video call in which Kelce gave Seydou some advice and convinced him to trust coach Jones and his staff. Seydou signed in February 2021 and transitioned to tight end, showing natural instincts for the position.

Traore saw himself as a "big ball of clay" that Jones could mould, and the coach says he was "like a sponge" in terms of retaining information.

"In his first year Seydou looked like a young deer that could run but hadn't really matured yet, grown into his body," adds Jones.

"By year two you could see that development. He made some plays where you were in awe on the sideline."

Like Kelce, Traore can hurdle defenders, and in 2022 he was named the best tight end in the Sun Belt Conference. But he was determined to step up to the top level of college football and play in one of the Power Four conferences.

Seydou spent early 2023 with Colorado, whose tight ends coach called him out during a news conference, questioning his "toughness" and work ethic.

"We talked a few times when he was at Colorado, going through some tough times," says Jones.

"There was a lot of adversity through his journey, but he never gave up. He had that mental disposition it takes, every single day, to fight off the doubt that can creep in, especially when you're away from home."

In those moments, Seydou thought about his family.

"Knowing what I'd left and what I was trying to become was very motivating," he says.

After a term at Colorado, Seydou felt it best for his development to move on and he went to Mississippi State, who play in college football's most prestigious conference, the Southeastern.

But because he had transferred twice in quick succession, NCAA rules meant he could not play during 2023. All he could do was train.

It was then that Seydou found out just how much he wanted it. He treated it as a chance to improve his game, and when he finally played for Mississippi State in 2024, he was one of their top receiving threats.

Then in 2025, he began to catch the eye of NFL scouts. He scored a career-high five touchdowns and became a fans' favourite for his new tea-sipping celebration, a nod to the British stereotype.

Seydou's family also visited twice, seeing him for the first time in five years and witnessing just how "crazy" American college sport is.

There was a military flyover, fireworks and a cacophony of cowbells among the 60,000 crowd - a long-held tradition at Mississippi State.

With Seydou's college career now complete, it was time to enter the NFL Draft.

NFL teams recruit their best players through the draft, a three-day process that has become one of the biggest events in the NFL calendar.

Each year about 260 players are selected across seven rounds. They get a call from their new team and a few minutes later their name is announced on stage. A record 805,000 fans attended this year's draft in Pittsburgh.

Hundreds of prospects are evaluated by NFL experts and Seydou was projected to be picked on the final day, when rounds four to seven take place.

Former player Efe Obada was there to support the international hopefuls. Having also gone from London Warriors to the NFL, he is an academy ambassador and saw Traore at the try-outs in 2019.

So after the Miami Dolphins called Traore late in the fifth round, Obada "kind of hijacked" his announcement.

He ran into the office NFL commissioner Roger Goodell was using and told him "I wanna do it". Goodell agreed it "made sense" and they went on stage together to welcome Traore into the NFL.

"I thought it would be symbolic, passing on the torch," says Obada. "I've kind of gone through that journey and I wanted people to know that it's a moment. [Being drafted] doesn't just happen. This sport is about endurance and commitment."

As a former London Warriors coach, Aden Durde was aware of Traore's talent before he too attended the first academy try-outs.

And the British defensive co-ordinator, who helped the Seattle Seahawks win the Super Bowl in February, smiled when he heard Traore's name mentioned during this year's pre-draft process.

"It's so cool to see him go to different colleges and really kick down the door and break barriers," he says.

"That was the vision of the NFL Academy all those years ago. He's the first one and there's going to be plenty more. It's exciting times."

Travis Clayton was the first ex-academy player to be drafted but only spent a brief period with the programme in 2019 and did not attend a US college, so Traore is the first of its alumni to follow the full pathway.

Since the academy's inception more than 75 students have secured college football scholarships in the US.

Traore has remained cool, calm and collected throughout his journey, even when he strode on to the NFL Draft stage. Draped in a British flag, he stopped to put on a Dolphins cap and do his tea-sipping celebration for the camera.

But one day in June, far from the draft spotlight, his excitement got the better of him.

Zeinab says they used to joke about who would be the first to buy their mum a house. Seydou knew he had won when he signed a four-year rookie contract worth $4.8m (£3.6m).

And it was his older sister, not his mum, whom he called to say "I'm signing right now!"

Not all drafted players are guaranteed to play from the start of their rookie season. Teams must whittle their roster from 90 or 91 players down to 53 by 31 August.

Traore is trying to earn a spot during Miami's training camp but is backing himself to continue his remarkable journey in the NFL.

"It feels good [to be here]," he adds. "But I keep telling everyone, it's just the beginning."

title: Four pointers to most open Premier League title race in years
description: Three of the Premier League's "big six" have new managers, the champions have a key injury issue and Tottenham and Chelsea are breaking transfer records - and that might mean a very open title race.
fullText:
Three of the traditional "big six" have new managers, the defending champions have a key injury and Tottenham and Chelsea are breaking transfer records.

After years of Manchester City dominance followed by Liverpool and Arsenal winning titles by at least seven points, the Premier League is due a wide open, unpredictable, multi-club title race.

Here are four reasons why 2026-27 could be that season.

How do you replace the irreplaceable?

Manchester City are often title favourites having won six of the past nine Premier League trophies, but they start this new season without their greatest ever manager, Pep Guardiola.

The 55-year-old led City to 17 major trophies in 10 years, but left at the end of last season and has since been replaced by his former assistant Enzo Maresca.

Maresca has been out of work since stepping down as Chelsea boss in January.

The Blues also have a new gaffer. They replaced Maresca with Liam Rosenior in January but he was let go before the end of the season and now former Liverpool player Xabi Alonso is at the helm.

Alonso won the Bundesliga with an invincible Bayer Leverkusen team two years ago but last term had a difficult spell in charge of Real Madrid.

Many thought he would replace 2024-25 title-winner Arne Slot at Liverpool but the Reds instead have appointed Andoni Iraola, who finished sixth with Bournemouth last season.

That's three huge clubs with three new managers.

What's more, Manchester United's Michael Carrick and Tottenham's Roberto de Zerbi only took charge part way through last season.

So five of the traditional big six will start to the new campaign with a different manager to the one they had at the start of last season.

Only Mikel Arteta of Arsenal, appointed in 2019, remains.

As defending champions and with an experienced manager, Arsenal are favourites for the Premier League title.

But a lengthy injury to a key starter could affect their title chances.

The club have said defender William Saliba is set to miss an "extended period" after suffering a back injury while at the World Cup with France.

Saliba, 25, made 50 appearances in all competitions for Arsenal last season and his formidable partnership with team-mate Gabriel was a big factor in them conceding fewer goals than anyone else in the division.

Arsenal have a tricky start to the season, facing Aston Villa and Chelsea in two of their first three matches.

Since Saliba's debut in 2022, Arsenal have won 68.7% of their Premier League matches when he has been in the team (131 games).

When he has been sidelined, that win percentage drops to 47.6% (21 games).

Last season, Manchester United played just 40 matches in all competitions, their fewest in a single campaign since 1914-15, and finished third.

Chelsea played 59 matches in all competitions and finished 10th.

Tottenham played 52 matches in all competitions and avoided relegation on the final day, finishing 17th.

Playing more matches does not always correlate with a lower league finish. Arsenal, for instance, won the Premier League title last season while reaching both the Champions League and Carabao Cup finals.

But fewer matches in other competitions does mean a team can rotate less, often have a full week of preparation between games and be less susceptible to injuries.

Spurs had a staggering 27 different players sidelined at some point last season.

Next season Chelsea and Tottenham are not playing European football whereas Manchester United and eight other Premier League clubs are.

United have responded by targeting midfielders in the transfer market, having bought Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans from Chelsea and Aston Villa respectfully.

But will those two additions be enough to cover the club's increased workload?

Chelsea and Tottenham both underperformed last season, but the pair could pick up this term after going big in the transfer window.

Chelsea made England midfielder Morgan Rogers the most expensive British player in history this month by signing him from Aston Villa for a fee of £117m.

They've also spent £47m on full-back Marco Palestra from Atalanta and are close to deals for Danny Welbeck, Jordan Henderson and Maxence Lacroix.

Tottenham have almost matched Chelsea's spending, parting with a club record £237m this summer.

In July, Spurs broke their transfer record twice in two days, first signing midfielder Mateus Fernandes from West Ham for £85m before bringing in Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m.

They've also picked up Jan Paul van Hecke, for £52m from Brighton, Marcos Senesi, Andrew Robertson and Martin Dubravka.

With so many new signings and different managers, who knows what to expect?

title: Fifa could receive first money from Infantino plan in October
description: Fifa could bank first lot of private World Cup cash by end of October as European football's governing body Uefa will hold a meeting of all 55 member associations on Thursday afternoon to discuss its response to controversial World Cup plans.
fullText:
Football's world governing body expects to receive the first funding generated by president Gianni Infantino's controversial sell-off plans by the end of October.

Infantino has proposed the creation of a subsidiary body to run Fifa tournaments, which would include some outside investment.

Fifa has given all 211 member associations until 19 September to say whether they agree with the plan, with a straight majority to decide whether to proceed.

One of the main complaints around the plan so far has been a lack of consultation.

Critics will say that is underlined by a new document sent to associations by Fifa - and seen by BBC Sport - outlining the following timescales around funding:

August: Investors given access to term sheet and select materials.

September: Investors indicate investment amount and confirm terms.

October: Commitment letters submitted, long-form agreements agreed, tender allocations made.

Late October: Investors transfer funds to Fifa by end of October.

The latest development comes as European football's governing body prepares to hold an emergency meeting on Thursday afternoon to discuss its response.

Uefa kept up its offensive over the plans after it was discovered Fifa had sent an earlier letter - also seen by the BBC - to every association giving them until 19 September to decide if they want to accept the deal, and with it the first $20m (£15m) of an initial $40m (£30m).

"We have learned of Fifa's deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn," said Uefa. "This says everything you need to know about this plan."

That was Uefa's second statement on the issue. The first claimed Fifa had "crossed a line".

It is not known precisely what will be discussed at the meeting, which will be held virtually.

Many of Fifa's members - including the Football Association - are furious at only learning through the media of the proposal to sell a 20% stake in Fifa competitions to private finance - led by the Thrive Eternal investment vehicle owned by Joshua Kushner, the brother-in-law of US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka.

FA chair Debbie Hewitt was among the Fifa vice-presidents not given advance notice. Uefa's unease has been echoed by the Asian, South American and North and Central American Confederations.

David Bernstein - a former chairman of both the FA and Manchester City - said England should "withdraw" from the World Cup if Infantino's proposals go through.

Three of the 2026 World Cup semi-finalists are among Uefa's 55 members. It knows the nuclear option of its members pulling out of the tournament would severely damage the financial viability of the concept.

That is very much viewed as the outer edge of what is possible, particularly as one Uefa member has said it is broadly in agreement with Infantino's proposals.

"We can see the pragmatic benefits for Czech football," said David Trunda - president of the Czech FA.

However, the World Leagues organisation, chaired by Premier League chief executive Richard Masters, feels Fifa is acting beyond its remit.

"Fifa's responsibilities extend beyond the commercial success of its own competitions," it said.

"While around 1% of the world's professional players participate in the World Cup, the other 130,000 professional footballers and all their clubs stop competing as national league competitions come to a halt."

It added the creation of a subsidiary body to control Fifa's commercial activities "further highlights the conflict of interest between Fifa's role as regulator of world football and the commercial organiser of major international competitions".

It concluded: "The World Leagues Association asks Fifa to withdraw its project and reiterates the need for a fundamental change in Fifa's decision-making processes."

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

After widespread condemnation of both the proposals and the manner in which they have been created, Fifa released an eight-page document highlighting the reasons behind them.

Fifa said its view was "too little of football's growing commercial value has reached the parts of the game that need it most".

It has been pointed out the sums being spoken about are more than some member associations spend annually and questions have been raised about the auditing of money Fifa already hands over in some parts of the world.

Despite this, Infantino feels the proposals would help provide funding for "better pitches, stronger national teams, more pathways for young players, and greater support for women's football".

In a video released by Fifa on Wednesday, Infantino defended the plans, calling them "an offer, not an obligation".

"It's part of a democratic process - a consultation process - and, above all, it is an opportunity but not an obligation," he added.

"It is a golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally."

Fifa points to the qualification of Cape Verde, Curacao, Jordan and Uzbekistan for the World Cup for the first time as an example of the positive benefits of its work, though that was, in part, due to the expansion of the competition to 48 teams.

It also cites Formula 1, La Liga, Ligue 1 and the Bundesliga as examples of other sporting organisations that use "dedicated commercial operations".

It says private investors would "absolutely not" have any influence over the World Cup.

There has been a stream of comment on the issue, most of it negative.

The European Leagues organisation said on Wednesday that Fifa's proposals represented "a reckless and divisive development for world football".

"The World Cup should not be for sale. It is not the Fifa president's private equity asset," a statement read.

Global players' union Fifpro called on Fifa to "reconsider its proposal without further delay".

It said it had "noted with deep concern the proposal to transform the World Cup and other Fifa competitions into investable assets for private capital".

Fifpro added such a move "would fundamentally and irreversibly reshape the incentives underpinning the competitions" and it was "particularly troubling that a project of this magnitude has been developed largely behind closed doors".

La Liga president Javier Tebas accused Infantino of trying to buy votes before the next Fifa congress in March.

"It doesn't seem like a reform. It seems like an electoral campaign financed with the future of football," Tebas said.

"Development cannot be used to buy votes or silences. The competitions and commercial rights of Fifa are not the personal patrimony of Infantino.

"Whoever mixes politics, discipline, money and power without transparency cannot lead anything.

"Infantino is not the solution to Fifa's governance. He is the problem."

Hans-Joachim Watzke - vice-president of the German Football Association (DFB) and president of Borussia Dortmund - told Kicker magazine Fifa's plans were an "absolute attack on football".

He said: "A line has been crossed here. If European football stands united against these plans, that carries a great deal of weight."

title: Phillips' struggles are a cautionary tale for Anderson
description: As Kalvin Phillips nears a fourth loan move away from Manchester City, what can record signing Elliot Anderson learn from his struggles at the Etihad?
fullText:
When Elliot Anderson completed his £116m move from Nottingham Forest to Manchester City last week, there was a sense of deja vu.

It is not the first time City has signed one of the most sought-after midfielders in the Premier League fresh from an impressive first international tournament with England.

A similar story unfolded in 2022 when Kalvin Phillips left his boyhood club, Leeds United, to join City on a six-year deal.

Fast forward four years and Phillips is on the brink of leaving the Etihad on loan for a fourth time, with the midfielder set to join Sheffield United for a second successive season.

So, is there anything Anderson can learn from Phillips' plight?

After spending eight seasons in the first team at Elland Road, Phillips helped Leeds secure Premier League survival a year after winning the Championship title.

His performances also earned him a key role in England's run to the European Championships final in 2021, with his move to the Etihad expected to take his career to the next level.

Instead, it marked arguably the most difficult period of his career.

When Phillips arrived at Manchester City ahead of the 2022-23 season, he faced the challenge of breaking into a midfield that had won the Premier League only a few months earlier.

That task became even harder when, after just one substitute appearance in the Premier League for his new club, he was ruled out for almost three months with a shoulder injury sustained in training.

Phillips was sidelined from September and, by the time he returned in November, domestic football was coming to a halt ahead of the World Cup in Qatar.

It left the England international competing with Rodri for a spot in midfield, with the Spain international further establishing himself as City's first-choice holding midfielder.

After making just two substitute appearances for England at the World Cup, Phillips returned in December to find himself out of City's squad for their first game back against Liverpool. Guardiola publicly accused him of being "overweight" and not fit enough to train or play.

The club went on to become the first English side in almost a quarter of a century to complete the treble, winning the Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League, with Rodri scoring the winner against Inter Milan in the latter.

In 2024, Phillips, then on loan at Ipswich Town, said Guardiola's comments about his weight had left him feeling "frustrated".

It would be easy to view Phillips' Manchester City career as a story of wasted talent and unfulfilled potential.

With the benefit of hindsight, the circumstances surrounding his £45m move in 2022 paint a more complicated picture.

Anderson is unlikely to face the same challenges during his debut season at City next term.

The club are set to enter a period of transition following Guardiola's departure at the end of last season, with Enzo Maresca appointed as his successor.

It is the biggest change City have faced since Guardiola arrived in 2016 and comes alongside the departures of several long-serving players, including John Stones and Bernardo Silva.

There is also uncertainty surrounding the future of Rodri, with reports in Spain linking the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner with a potential move to Real Madrid.

In 2022, City were fresh from back-to-back Premier League titles and Phillips was expected to compete for a place in midfield with Rodri, who was establishing himself as one of the best players in the world in that position.

However, Anderson faces a different challenge.

As the second most expensive British player of all time, his move to the Etihad has attracted significant attention.

The 23-year-old will be aware of the scrutiny he will face and can use Phillips' struggles as a reminder of the demands that come with playing for one of the biggest clubs in the Premier League.

For Anderson, the next step is adapting quickly to life at City and showing he can become an important part of the club's new era.

Subscribe and listen for everything you love about City

Phillips' stock was at its highest when he was named England's player of the year at the end of the 2020-21 campaign.

He continued that form with Leeds United before Manchester City decided to pay £45m to sign the player the following summer but his Blues career never took off.

He played only one Premier League game before the 2022 World Cup and it was Guardiola's comments following the tournament which Phillips never really recovered from.

The midfielder attempted to re-ignite his career but endured unsuccessful spells at West Ham and Ipswich over the next two seasons.

There was a brief return in a City shirt last September when he featured for the final seven minutes of a Carabao Cup tie victory at Huddersfield, but it proved to be a false dawn.

A return to Sheffield United again this summer is Phillips' latest attempt to revive his career.

title: De Zerbi wants to convince Spence to stay at Spurs
description: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says he wants to convince England defender Djed Spence to stay at the club.
fullText:
Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says he wants to convince England defender Djed Spence to stay at the club amid uncertainty over his future.

The 25-year-old, who signed a long-term deal with the club last year, has been linked with a move to Inter Milan and Everton.

De Zerbi says he sees Spence as an important part of his plans despite increased competition in his role after a summer of significant spending.

Spurs have spent a club record £237m so far this summer as they rebuild their squad after narrowly avoiding relegation on the final day of last season's Premier League.

"I repeat what I said to Djed, and to Lucas [Bergvall]," De Zerbi said, referencing comments he made about the in-demand Sweden midfielder a day earlier.

"I would like you to stay if you want to stay. If you don't want to stay, if you want to leave, then you have to leave."

Spence started in 23 of his 30 Premier League appearances last year as Spurs finished 17th for the second season in a row.

Spain's World Cup winner Pedro Porro currently occupies Spence's preferred right-back position at Tottenham.

De Zerbi said he regarded Porro as the "best in the world" in his role.

In-demand Bergvall starts for Spurs, but De Zerbi 'can't give guarantee'

Latest Tottenham news, analysis and fan views

Ask about Tottenham - what do you want to know?

Captain Cristian Romero is among those likely to leave the club.

Romero was criticised for his decision to fly back to Argentina while injured before the final game of the season - a match for which he did ultimately return.

De Zerbi said it was wrong to criticise Romero for his initial decision, saying he had shown "unbelievable behaviour" during the Italian's time at the club, but accepted it was "his will" to leave.

"At the beginning of my time in April I had, I don't know, one million individual meetings. And the players told me if they are (staying) here (or not)," he said.

"I said: 'Yes, help me to stay up, and then I help you to leave. If you don't help me to stay up, you stay underwater with me.'"

Italian goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario is also expected to depart after losing his place to Antonin Kinsky.

Earlier this month, Spurs broke their transfer record twice in two days, first signing midfielder Mateus Fernandes from West Ham for £85m before bringing in Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m.

Jan Paul van Hecke has also joined from Brighton in a £52m deal, alongside the free transfers of experienced trio Marcos Senesi, Andrew Robertson and Martin Dubravka.

De Zerbi says his side are targeting another attacking signing alongside their pursuit of Manchester City's Savinho.

The Brazilian is among the attacking players in advanced talks over a move to north London, with Spurs also pursuing another unnamed target.

Speaking in Sydney, De Zerbi said: "The transfer market is not finished for sure, but we have completed 60% of our project. Now we have another 'bomba'."

Asked whether he was referring to a winger or a striker, the former Brighton and Marseille manager replied: "Attackers.

"I don't love working with plan A, plan B, plan C. It is plan A, full stop, because all players are not the same.

"We have to increase the number of goals."

De Zerbi said he had been like a "shark" this summer while pursuing targets.

De Zerbi omitted the name of the player by design - but it will leave Spurs fans guessing as to who it could be.

Arguably the biggest available name is Paris St-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, who is valued at more than £140m and is exploring his options away from the European champions. Liverpool are believed to be preparing an opening bid for the France international, who has also been on Arsenal's radar.

Manchester United forward Marcus Rashford has a £40m release clause in his contract, although his £325,000-a-week deal, which runs until 2028, could prove a stumbling block.

There is also a sense that, following his loan spell at Barcelona, the England international would prefer another move abroad after the Spanish champions opted against triggering a £26m option to buy.

Other potential targets could include Galatasaray striker Victor Osimhen, Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, Chelsea's Pedro Neto or AC Milan winger Rafael Leao.

However, any suggestion remains speculative until Spurs reveal their hand or one of the clubs involved confirms an approach from chief executive Vinai Venkatesham and sporting director Johan Lange.

title: Howe going as spending rules bite - troubles for Newcastle's Saudi owners
description: Newcastle United wanted to become one of the world's top clubs under their Saudi owners - but Eddie Howe's decision to leave is a sign of the troubles they are facing.
fullText:
Seven months ago, Newcastle United's chief executive David Hopkinson said he could put them "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.

Right now, that ambition looks a long way off.

The departure of manager Eddie Howe on Thursday, and reported appointment of Matthias Jaissle, is the result of a poor Premier League season, where Newcastle finished 12th, and an uninspiring transfer window.

The latter is in no small part down to the club's need to sell players to generate income and so be able to spend more.

But does this latest development point to a bigger issue?

Newcastle have let go some of their biggest players in Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali while captain Bruno Guimaraes is also rumoured to be on his way out. That follows the £125m sale of striker Alexander Isak to Liverpool last September.

Transfers the other way have not exactly been flooding in either, with Newcastle missing out on Swiss midfielder Johan Manzambi to Aston Villa and Spanish winger Victor Munoz to Liverpool.

Newcastle's Saudi Arabia-backed takeover in 2021 - by the Public Investment Fund (PIF) - was supposed to lead to them becoming one of the world's top clubs.

But recent actions have raised questions about whether they are running out of steam.

Where are Newcastle in bid to be the best by 2030?

The winner who played for Tuchel - potential Newcastle boss Jaissle

Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when his side won the Carabao Cup last year.

But rumours about the 48-year-old's departure have been circulating since the beginning of this year, when Newcastle sat 13th in the Premier League and securing Champions League football for next season was already starting to look highly unlikely.

That was exacerbated further in March when the Magpies were struck by a late Sunderland comeback in the Tyne-Wear derby, losing 2-1 at St James' Park, to extend their dismal league record against their local rivals to 15 years without victory.

They also went out of the FA Cup in the fifth round, exited the Champions League in the last 16 and made it to the semi-finals of the EFL Cup only to be beaten 5-1 by Manchester City over two legs.

Despite that, Howe's four-and-a-half-year stint as Newcastle boss will be looked back on fondly by Newcastle fans.

What supporters will perhaps be most perplexed by is the timing of Howe's departure.

The former Bournemouth boss could have left at the end of the season and would probably have been given a positive send off by fans.

Instead, Howe got partway through pre-season before making his decision, the difficulties of building a squad he is happy with having become too much.

Although he understood the situation - saying in March "there's a limit to what we can spend" despite the ambition of the club - it is understood he communicated his intent to leave two weeks ago.

Selling three of your best players in the space of one year - Isak to Liverpool last summer and this year Gordon at Barcelona and Tonali to Tottenham - with another one possibly on the way in Guimaraes, is perhaps not conducive to becoming a top club.

Former Newcastle defender Steve Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle: "I'm shocked but at the same time kind of not.

"Eddie for a long time has basically had to put fires out. You are losing your best players.

"You can understand the frustration with him when he's trying to build something but you're having that semi-taken away losing your best players. It's always going to be difficult.

"You can understand his frustration."

So what are the rules that Newcastle have, at times, come close to breaking?

From the beginning of the PIF takeover, Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) have put the brakes on Newcastle's ambitions to spend.

Just because a club has wealthy owners does not mean they can spend big in the transfer windows.

After buying the club in 2021, PIF spent £404.7m in the first three years. But by bringing in only £50.4m from sales, Newcastle saw the stark reality of PSR hit home in 2024.

That led to them having to sell homegrown talent Elliot Anderson to Nottingham Forest and has snowballed since, with important players being offloaded every season.

The Magpies welcomed the new Financial Fair Play rules - the Squad Cost Ratio (SCR), which are now in effect - and, in short, mean the more you generate, the more you can spend.

But, when analysing their spending power against that of other Premier League clubs, Swiss Ramble, external found that the Magpies' SCR budget ranked ninth (£243m) in the Premier League.

On top of that, in April the PIF withdrew its multibillion dollar backing of LIV Golf after Yasir Al-Rumayyan - the fund's governor and chairman of Newcastle - confirmed the PIF was reviewing its deals and investments.

In turn, questions were raised about what that meant for the future of Newcastle - but senior club figures were informed at the time that the pullout did not affect the club. The fund is still viewed as being engaged.

In the club's most recent set of accounts from last season, Newcastle's revenues have more than doubled to £335.3m - from the £140.2m recorded in the final full campaign of Mike Ashley's ownership.

There are also plans for a new state-of-the-art training ground while Hopkinson has outlined a desire to revamp St James' Park or move stadiums to increase matchday revenue.

The potential appointment of former RB Salzburg boss Jaissle is also intriguing given he is currently in charge of Saudi Arabian side Al-Ahli - a club the PIF held a majority stake in until selling it in April.

It is understood that Howe communicated his intention to leave to the Newcastle hierarchy around a fortnight ago.

Newcastle initially asked him to reconsider to continue leading the club into next season.

Eventually, though, Newcastle accepted Howe's wishes but asked him to stay as they identified his replacement - a request the coach accepted.

Plenty has been made about the club's transfer policy this summer.

BBC Sport outlined in April how Newcastle would need to sell at least one of their top players during the current transfer window to comply with financial regulations.

Indeed, Howe leaves amid a backdrop of high-profile departures and in terms of incomings, Newcastle are going for younger, unproven talents – with the likes of relatively unknown Bazoumana Traore and Aladji Bamba arriving.

But while it is BBC Sport's understanding that the transfer strategy has prompted concern at how the squad is shaping up for next season and how competitive it may be, it is claimed that alone is not the only factor in Howe's decision to quit, and that the split between both parties is amicable.

title: 'Ready to write Chelsea story' - Lacroix makes £52m move
description: Chelsea sign France World Cup defender Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace for £52m.
fullText:
Chelsea have signed France's World Cup defender Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace for £52m.

The 26-year-old, capped seven times by France, has penned a contract at Stamford Bridge until 2032.

The Frenchman joined Palace from Bundesliga side Wolfsburg in 2024 for an initial £15.5m and became a regular under Oliver Glasner last season.

Lacroix made 55 appearances in all competitions as Palace won the Uefa Conference League, the club's first major European trophy.

The defender made three appearances for France during the 2026 World Cup, including against England in the third-place play-off, as Les Bleus finished fourth.

"I think when I saw the players like Reece [James], like Morgan [Rogers], I'm just really happy to be also in a way in their story, you know? To write part of the Chelsea story with them," Lacroix said.

"I'm really proud, really happy, to be part of this beautiful project and I just want to start playing.

"I'm really excited to see the guys, to see the manager, to start the season, because I feel like we have a story to write here, and I can be part of it, so it's beautiful."

Lacroix is Chelsea's third signing of the summer transfer window, joining Morgan Rogers and Marco Palestra in moving to west London, as the club prepares for its first season under new boss Xabi Alonso.

Deals for winger Geovany Quenda and forward Emmanuel Emegha were agreed in 2025, with both players formally completing moves this month.

The Blues are also currently in talks to sign Brighton striker Danny Welbeck and Brentford midfielder Jordan Henderson.

Lacroix had been on a shortlist of centre-back options since it became clear Chelsea's defence was underperforming and that they needed more physicality and leadership in their backline.

Although former Manchester City defender John Stones and Como's Jacobo Ramon were also known to be under consideration, it always felt as though the 6ft 4in Palace defender was Chelsea's preferred target.

Lengthy negotiations over both personal terms and the transfer fee with Crystal Palace added uncertainty to the deal.

However, Lacroix gave the move the green light last week after France's World Cup campaign ended with a fourth-place finish following defeat by England in the bronze-medal match.

The signing offers a glimpse into Chelsea's future direction after a season in which they finished 10th in the Premier League and ended the campaign without a trophy, prompting frustration among supporters.

Co-owner Behdad Eghbali said Chelsea would "tweak" their model and add experience to what he still believes is a strong core of young players including Cole Palmer, Moises Caicedo and Levi Colwill.

Not only is Lacroix the oldest player signed under the current ownership since Eghbali and his sporting directors took control, but Chelsea also attempted to sign Granit Xhaka, 34, from Sunderland in a deal that would have been highly unusual for the club's recruitment strategy.

Although Chelsea were unable to reunite the Switzerland midfielder with his former Bayer Leverkusen manager Alonso, the attempt sent a clear message that the club's approach is changing.

Along with £117m arrival Rogers, who turned 24 on Saturday, Lacroix's arrival means Chelsea have delivered on their pledge to make at least two ready-made signings.

title: Fleming new England Test coach with Root captain
description: Former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming is appointed as England Test coach, with Joe Root as captain.
fullText:
Former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming has been appointed as England Test coach, with Joe Root returning as captain.

Fleming, 53, has never previously worked as head coach of a national team but he led Chennai Super Kings to a record five Indian Premier League titles during his 17-year tenure as head coach.

Previous Test coach Brendon McCullum was fired earlier this month following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents, but remains in charge of England's white-ball sides.

Root, 35, whose first spell as Test captain was between 2017 and 2022, captained England to a record 27 Test wins in 65 matches.

He has been reappointed captain following the shock retirement of Ben Stokes from international cricket in June.

Fleming said he was "incredibly excited" to be taking on the role as Test coach.

"It's one of the most prestigious coaching positions in world cricket and I am honoured to be appointed," he added.

Fleming will not be in charge for the Test series against Pakistan, which begins on 19 August. Assistant coach Marcus Trescothick will be the interim head coach.

Fleming will spend time with his family in New Zealand before flying to the UK later this summer to begin preparations for the South Africa Test tour in December.

Root said taking on the captain's role alongside Fleming was a "huge motivator".

He added: "[Fleming] has proved over a long period of time that he is an exceptional leader with a great knowledge of the game, and I am looking forward to working with him and helping to build a winning environment."

Fleming will inherit a side that saw its momentum falter after a breathtaking start to the McCullum era.

McCullum won 10 out of 12 Tests in his first year in charge but since then, England have lost 18 and won 17 of 37 Tests.

They have not won a multi-match series since December 2024.

The decision to remove McCullum came after the 4-1 Ashes hammering in Australia was followed by a 2-1 home series defeat by New Zealand, including Stokes announcing his retirement during play in the third Test.

Root made his Test debut in 2012 and holds several England Test cricket records, including highest run scorer with 14,114 runs. He is also second highest run-scorer of all time behind India legend Sachin Tendulkar, who is top with 15,921 runs.

He took over the captaincy for the first time when Alastair Cook stepped down from the role in 2017.

Fleming called Root a "generational talent who has achieved so much already", adding: "I'm excited to support him so he can enjoy and thrive in the role in what is a different context to his first stint."

Gavin Hamilton, director of cricket at Yorkshire, said Root "raises the standards" whenever he returns to his club, with young players learning "simply by watching the way he way he prepares, trains and competes".

Fleming, who retired as a player in 2009, has a wealth of experience in Test cricket as a player, making 111 appearances for New Zealand, scoring 7,172 runs at 40.06, and remains the Black Caps' most successful captain with 28 wins from 80 matches.

He also spent time in England in the county game, playing for Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire - where he won the County Championship in 2005.

"Of course, the ambition is always to win now. But equally, it's about ensuring the team is well placed for the medium and long-term future," said Fleming.

"There is a lot of young talent in and around the team and our aim is to help them fulfil their potential as world-class cricketers."

Former Test captain Stokes announced his retirement from international cricket on the fourth day of the deciding Test against New Zealand at Trent Bridge.

The shock decision came after he returned to duty following the fall-out from a London nightclub incident where team-mate Gus Atkinson was also present earlier that month.

Stokes, 35, had backed Harry Brook to succeed him in the role, but the 27-year-old, who leads the white-ball sides, was overlooked for the role earlier in the summer.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald says Stokes has "a lot of good cricket left in him" and believes Fleming should entice him out of international retirement for the Ashes next year.

"The fairytale would be that he comes back out of retirement and takes on one more Ashes and builds a lot of hype on the way in," McDonald told Australian radio station SEN on Wednesday, before Fleming's confirmation as coach.

"If you're looking at promoting that series, that's probably the angle that you would want, that he comes out of retirement.

"To me, he's still got a lot of good cricket left in him."

Root's return is a fascinating one, though perhaps not overly surprising given the lack of viable options available.

Brook has the responsibility of leading the young England white-ball sides, and was overlooked earlier in the summer when Stokes missed the second Test against New Zealand at the Oval in the fall-out from breaking a curfew after the win at Lord's.

Other choices could have seen Jacob Bethell or Ben Duckett as captain, but these seemed far-fetched given a lack of leadership experience.

What will be interesting is whether Root's leadership style has changed in the four years since giving up the job the first time. His captaincy towards the end of his previous tenure was marked by criticisms of a timid approach that failed to bring the best from England's batting talents.

Will the 'Bazball' mentality that saw Root reverse scooping the first ball of the day in an Ashes Test remain, or is it more likely English Test cricket will see a return to some sense of normality? A balance is probably best for all concerned.

As for Fleming, his close relationship with McCullum could be crucial. The two have described each other as "great mates" and even share business interests. Given the pressures on balancing the demands of the white-ball and red-ball sides, this link is clearly a valuable one.

There has seldom been a time when both the Test and white-ball sides have shared concurrent success - could this Kiwi combination finally make that happen?

title: The winner who played for Tuchel - potential Newcastle boss Jaissle
description: German Matthias Jaissle is the favourite to replace Eddie Howe at Newcastle - and has a reputation for attacking football and winning trophies.
fullText:
Matthias Jaissle is the surprise favourite to take over as Newcastle head coach as Eddie Howe's replacement - and would arrive with a strong recent record of success.

Howe, 48, is set to leave St James' Park after nearly five years. He had been in charge since November 2021 when he replaced Steve Bruce and took the Magpies to their first domestic trophy in 70 years by winning the Carabao Cup in 2025.

Former RB Salzburg boss Jaissle, currently in charge of Saudi Arabian side Al-Ahli, is now expected to come in.

The 38-year-old German was a centre-half, progressing through the Stuttgart youth system before playing senior football for Hoffenheim from 2007 to 2014.

He represented Germany at Under-21 level, but was forced to retire through injury at the age of 25.

Jaissle took his first coaching steps as assistant manager of Danish club Brondby between 2017 and 2019. He then took over RB Salzburg's Under-18 academy team before becoming a head coach for the first time at Liefering in Austria's second tier.

He guided them to a second-placed finish, the club's joint best-ever position, and that achievement helped him become RB Salzburg manager in 2021, replacing Jesse Marsch, who would later manage Leeds United and then Canada at the 2026 World Cup.

In two seasons with RB Salzburg, Jaissle won the Austrian Bundesliga twice and also the Austrian Cup once.

Their team included Benjamin Sesko and Brenden Aaronson, who now play in the Premier League with Manchester United and Leeds United respectively, and German forward Karim Adeyemi, now at Barcelona.

Jaissle joined Saudi club Al-Ahli in 2023 and led them to consecutive Asian Champions League titles in 2025 and 2026. Such success would have been noted by Newcastle's Saudi ownership in the event of Howe leaving St James' Park.

Magpies supporters will be encouraged by Jaissle's methods - his teams play high-pressing attacking football. He demands they show intensity and force turnovers as high up the pitch as possible.

'Howe's perspective changed' - analysis as Newcastle manager leaves club

Howe to leave Newcastle with Jaissle expected to replace him

Al-Ahli's side include England striker Ivan Toney, Brazil defender Roger Ibanez and former Chelsea goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

England boss Thomas Tuchel was a youth coach at Stuttgart when Jaissle was a player there and the pair spoke before Toney was included in the Three Lions' World Cup squad this summer.

"I had fantastic feedback from his club coach, who was my player and I have a close connection with him," said Tuchel after naming his squad.

Newcastle fans would be hoping Jaissle could also help convince 30-year-old Toney to return to the Premier League after two years playing in Saudi Arabia.

Last summer, striker Alexander Isak moved to Liverpool at the end of the transfer window for a British record of £125m and Newcastle then lost two key players this summer - Sandro Tonali to Tottenham and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, while Arsenal are chasing captain Bruno Guimaraes.

Newcastle finished 12th in the Premier League last season, missing out on European football for 2026-27, and lost 4-1 to Championship side Bristol City in a pre-season friendly on Wednesday.

The Magpies begin their league campaign at home against Liverpool on Sunday, 23 August.

description:

Soon we can add A Line Held Tight, a visual novel that puts workers’ rights – and workers’ lives – at the very centre of the narrative.
