title: 10 Shows Like 'Futurama' You Should Watch Next
description: More shows filled with animated action and sci-fi silliness.
fullText:
After two cancellations and four so-called series finales and counting, Futurama might be the most resilient show ever. Another new season is on the way from Hulu, plus a series of (just announced) specials. If it doesn't have the consistent staying power of something like The Simpsons (with which it shares a creator in Matt Groening), Family Guy, or Bob's Burgers, it's got a pluckiness that makes it all the more charming. Plus, those shows have never made me ugly cry like that one episode about Fry's dog.

If you're looking for other shows that deliver similar sci-fi silliness, or you just want to get set with a backup in case Futurama gets cancelled again, these 10 genre comedies will be just the thing.

More cynical than Futurama (which is saying a fair bit), Rick & Morty nonetheless plays in the same high-concept sci-fi sandbox; both shows excel at a stupid/smart blend of comedy. Rick Sanchez is an old-school mad scientist (think Doc Brown, but drunker) dragging his well-meaning but hapless grandson on adventures in time and space, as well as across dimensions—Back to the Future meets Doctor Who, but crasser and far weirder. It's clever, gross, frequently disturbing, and occasionally a bit emotional—but mostly it's a wild good time exploring the multiverse. Stream Rick and Morty on Hulu and HBO Max.

Instead of focusing on the upper ranks of any given Federation starship, Star Trek: Lower Decks deals with the, well, lower decks—the crew behind the scenes that keeps everything going on a second-rate ship specializing in "Second Contact"—i.e. arriving after the main event to make sure all the paperwork is signed. It's a sitcom in space that still manages to feel like real Star Trek by balancing cartoon wackiness with convincing character arcs. By the end of Lower Decks' five seasons, the two-dimensional crew of the Cerritos feels as real as that of any other show in the franchise. Stream Star Trek: Lower Decks on Paramount+.

One of the closest analogues to Futurama is set in Japan's past—we're in late Edo-period Japan (roughly the early/mid-1800s) but, in this version of history, aliens have invaded, the shogun has surrendered, and samurai are outlawed. The eccentric Gintoki Sakata takes on a teenage apprentice in his business making deliveries and doing odd jobs, later joined by a teenage alien. There are long-running plot threads and weighty character arcs, but that's all balanced by often over-the-top, and just as often very funny, comedy that's variously smart, raunchy, and goofy. Characters break the fourth wall to crack jokes, and the show mercilessly parodies pop culture, including other popular anime. Stream Gintama on Hulu and Netflix.

Sharing a Hulu home with Futurama and coming from the Rick & Morty creators, Solar Opposites follows Korvo (Dan Stevens), Terry (Thomas Middleditch), Yumyulack (Sean Giambrone), and Jesse (Mary Mack), aliens from a once-advanced planet destroyed by an asteroid. The humor is very R&M-esque, including running side stories about shrunken humans and alien cops, but there's a bit more sincerity here; the show satirizes human culture while making clear that it's not always fun to be a refugee. Stream Solar Opposites on Hulu and Netflix.

This much-loved, if relatively short-lived, animated series follows twin siblings Mabel and Dipper Pines (Kristen Schaal and Jason Ritter) as they are sent to spend the summer with their great-uncle (aka "Grunkle") Stan (voiced by show creator Alex Hirsch). While helping Stan run his mystery-themed tourist shack, the kids tackle a series of supernatural mysteries, many related to the show's ultimate antagonist, dream demon Bill Cipher. If it's not exactly Futurama-style sci-fi, the X-Files inspiration is certainly prominent. Stream Gravity Falls on Disney+.

Seth MacFarlane's The Orville began life as a slightly scatological Star Trek parody—a show with a reverence for The Next Generation but also jizz jokes. It quickly grew into something more interesting, as MacFarlane's obvious affection for the franchise sent the show off in a more serious direction. Certainly by the Hulu-produced third season, it had become one of the most ambitious (still a bit silly) sci-fi shows on the air. A fourth season is allegedly on the way, though I'll believe it when I see it. Stream The Orville on Hulu.

The Planet Express isn't exactly a luxury liner, but Avenue 5 most certainly is. It's an interplanetary cruise ship headed by its popular captain, Ryan Clark (Hugh Laurie), and owned by obnoxious, eccentric billionaire Herman Judd (Josh Gadd). A minuscule shift sends the ship off course, such that the planned months-long jaunt will take three years, even though supplies won't last. It doesn't take long before the ship's pocket of civilization breaks down, with crew and passengers alike jockeying for power, or just food. Veep's Armando Iannucci is the creator and showrunner, and if you're familiar with that show, you'll recognize the general tone: dark comedy and a dim view of people under pressure, particularly the rich and powerful. Stream Avenue 5 on HBO Max.

What if the Futurama characters were all sort of effortlessly cool? OK, that's a big "if," but if this isn't quite a vibe match, there are some similarities, in the sense that we're dealing with a ragtag crew of odd jobbers—among them a woman out of time, awakened from a long cryogenic suspension she'd never agreed to. An iconic genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, comedy, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack. The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Not science fiction, but this fantasy riff also comes from Matt Groening and company; the art style and sense of humor are very similar, as are the voice actors, many of whom (including John DiMaggio and Lauren Tom) are direct transplants from Futurama. Oh, and there's also a brief appearance from the crew via crystal ball, so the shows would appear to be set in the same universe. Abbi Jacobson is Bean, the hard-drinking, hard-living princess of Dreamland, who joins up with Elfo the half-elf and Luci, her personal demon, for a series of increasingly strange adventures. It starts out amiably enough, but the serialization and contained story set it apart from other Matt Groening shows. Stream Disenchantment on Netflix.

Another scrappy sci-fi comedy that's returned from the dead multiple times—and may yet again. Craig Charles is Dave Lister, amiable loser and well-meaning slob who holds the lowest job possible on the enormous mining ship Red Dwarf (if Fry's your guy, you'll love Lister). When he sneaks a pregnant cat aboard, he's punished by being placed in suspended animation (without pay) for the rest of the trip. Which is a lot longer than anyone anticipated: When Dave wakes up, three million years have passed, and humanity is entirely extinct. The kittens survived and sired an inbred cat empire that's since risen and all but fallen, while the senile main computer has recreated Dave's hated roommate (Chris Barrie) as a hologram to keep him company. Soon joined by a prissy android, they spend the next 30+ years bumming about in space and stumbling into adventures—some of them involving cross-time and/or universe encounters with Kristine Kochanski, the Leela-esque object of Dave's (mostly) unrequited affection. Stream Red Dwarf on Britbox.

title: This App Is (Sort of) Bringing Back Samsung Messages
description: This new app recreates the experience of Samsung Messages, now with RCS.
fullText:
Earlier this month, Samsung officially killed off its proprietary messaging app. It wasn't much of a surprise. The company had announced the end of Samsung Messages back in April, and, before that, had slowly distanced itself from the app by keeping it off new Galaxy phones by default. If you have a newer Galaxy phone, it's possible you didn't even use Samsung Messages at the time of deprecation. But for legacy users, the app's retirement was sad and frustrating, as the only viable option to retain features and message history is Google Messages—a fine enough chat app, but yet another Google product Galaxy users must rely on.

As reported by Android Authority, app developer OzarksMade wants to continue Samsung Messages' legacy. Rather than keep the original app running, OzarksMade created a new messaging app that mimics the look and feel of Samsung Messages: Messages by OzarksMade. The new app is designed with both Samsung Messages and One UI in mind: To the untrained eye, not only does this look like a Samsung Galaxy app, it looks like Samsung Messages.

Messages by OzarksMade also adds RCS support in the app. There is a catch, however: While you can send and receive RCS messages in Messages by OzarksMade, you'll need to tap into Google Messages via Messages by OzarksMade's "Companion Mode." You won't have to use Google Messages itself, but it will be powering RCS in the new app. You don't have to use Companion Mode, and can eschew Google Messages altogether, but you will be limited to SMS and MMS—the true Samsung Messages experience.

While you should be mindful of making any new chat app your default messaging provider, OzarksMade does say that all messages remain on-device, so it shouldn't store your texts on its servers. In addition, OzarksMade says it takes anonymous information for statistics purposes only, including "a random identifier that is generated on your device, the app's version and release channel, your device model, and your Android version." However, as Android Authority points out, this app closely resembles Samsung's own products, and the company may seek to shut the app down should it feel OzarksMade infringed on any copyrights.

This new app isn't out just yet, as it will launch on Thursday, Aug. 13. If you're interested, you'll need to join Messages by OzarksMade's beta, which is currently ongoing. title: 10 Hacks Every Even Realities G2 Smart Glasses User Should Know
description: Turn your G2 smart glasses into a personal subtitle generator, a second brain, and more.
fullText:
Even Realities G2 glasses are the most hacker-friendly spectacles on the planet, and it's not even close. They're unassuming enough that nobody clocks you as the guy wearing a face-computer, but there's a ton happening behind the silent display. Out of the box, you can translate, navigate, talk to AI, and do other expected smart-glasses stuff, but Even Hub takes it further. Even Realities opened up a real developer platform that lets anyone build whatever they want for their glasses and share it with everyone else. Hackers, rejoice. Here are ten hacks for your G2s, comprising useful and wondrous Even Hub apps, five-minute installs and tweaks, and weekend-long projects that will test your coding skills and capacity for frustration. There's a second brain that remembers what most AI forgets, a sneaky way to make yourself insufferably good at trivia, and even an option for a second career as a magician.

This project really highlights the possibilities of Even Realities glasses. G2's come with Even AI ready to go, but you're not limited to it. Not only can you use the settings in the app to redirect the AI to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or another LLM, you can build a custom AI for your needs. For instance, Constella founder Tejas Sharma was frustrated by Even AI's inability to remember things, so they built a "second brain" by re-routing the AI to a layered version of Constella (an open knowledge base) running on their network.

Running Second Brain instead of Even AI means you can say something like, "Remember to pick up the dry cleaning every Wednesday," and it will be saved to your knowledge base. Later you can ask, "what was I supposed to do on Wednesday?" out loud, and a full AI agent searches your memory (using hybrid vector and keyword search), pulls in your connected tools if relevant, and hands you back a real composed answer formatted to fit cleanly on the lens.

You can also use meeting mode, where your glasses stream your mic and transcribe what's said onto the lens seconds behind the conversation. While you're still talking, the backend quietly digs through your memory, follows relevant connections, checks the web if it's useful, and surfaces a synthesized insight—which is a little like thinking. So if you're in a meeting and a coworker says, "Can we push the squash game until Wednesday?" your glasses cross-reference the statement against your memory in the background and silently surface: "Wednesday is dry cleaning pickup."

Second Brain was uploaded to the G2's Even Hub so you could use it as is, but Sharma's put the whole integration layer on GitHub, so if you're comfortable with some Python, you can see exactly how it talks to the glasses and build a variant on top of your own knowledge base.

We all know we should be using two-factor authentication (2FA), but grabbing your phone, unlocking it, and pulling up Messenger every time you want to log into Slack is a pain. There are two ways to make this easier:

No software method: Open the Even app on your phone, go to Settings > Notifications, and enable notifications. When an SMS message arrives, you'll be able to read the number floating in front of you. Type it in and you "two-factored" without pulling out your phone.

The software solution: A developer in the Even Realities community created a dedicated app for this, 2Factor. Instead of waiting for a ping, you scan your 2FA QR codes into the app during setup. When it's time to log in, you can pull up your constantly updating, time-based OTP (one-time password) tokens directly from the glasses' menu. It is essentially Google Authenticator built straight into your eyeballs.

If you use autonomous AI coding agent Claude Code to build software, you know the biggest hassle isn't the AI writing the code, it's "babysitting" it. AI agents constantly pause to request permission before executing commands or editing files, tethering you to your keyboard with the simple job of saying, "yes" or "no." With the G2’s native Terminal Mode, you can mirror your computer’s terminal directly onto your glasses and act as a supervisor while grabbing coffee, pacing the room, or knitting.

Install the CLI bridge: On your computer, open your terminal and install the official Even package globally: npm install -g @evenrealities/even-terminal.

Launch your session: Start your AI coding agent on your computer, then run even-terminal. A pairing QR code will print directly inside your terminal window.

Pair your glasses: Open the Even Realities app on your phone, go to Settings > Terminal Mode, and scan the QR code off your computer screen to link the session.

Supervise on the move: Your computer's live terminal logs will now stream straight to your heads-up display in real time. Whenever your AI agent hits a checkpoint or asks for permission to execute a script, the prompt pops up in your line of sight—allowing you to approve the action using voice commands or glasses gestures so the build keeps moving forward.

If you're panicking because you've been invited to a traditional chakai tea gathering in Kanazawa tomorrow, and you don't know anything about Japanese etiquette, try Ojigi Coach. It's an app from the Even Hub that offers in-depth training and practice for ojigi, Japanese bowing. You'll learn the correct angle for each of the three main bow types, how long to keep your head down, and what situations call for you to bust out an eshaku, a keirei, or a saikeirei.

That would be enough, but it also lets you test your bowing skills by presenting real-life choose-a-bow situations like "you greet your boss in the morning" or "you meet a former teacher after a long time." You bow, then your glasses' accelerometer and inertial measurement unit track your bow's angle and duration and offer you pointers. It's not only a fascinating glimpse into a tiny aspect of another culture, but it's fun: trying to get your bows correct is a blast. Ojigi Coach is representative of many of the most interesting apps on the Even Hub: perhaps not obviously useful to many people, but essential to a few.

The standard G2 Translate app is geared for bilingual conversations, but there's a simple way to turn it into a private subtitle machine for foreign films, anime, and TV shows: open the Translate app, set the language, and start watching a Korean soap opera. But you can make it even better.

Switch your mic 

Place your phone: Set your phone down near your TV's soundbar or your laptop's speakers so it can capture the cleanest audio.

Pro tip: If you want to learn the language of the movie you're watching, give your glasses' touchpad a single tap. This toggles the display from "Half-Screen" (just the translation) to "Full-Screen" (which shows both the original foreign text and your translated text simultaneously).

Not only does this let you understand a foreign language, but you can use the same microphone hack to "hear" a TV in a noisy place. Set Translate to "English to English" (or use Conversate), then set your phone next to a distant TV speaker, and you'll be able to "hear" the TV from anywhere nearby.

Remember how Spock used to talk to the ship's computer in Star Trek? It's finally real. Even Hub app OcuClaw is a native OpenClaw client built for the G2. If you install one Claw on your glasses and the other on your PC or Mac, you can give your G2's AI the ability to interact directly with your computer's operating system. Once it's set up, you can use the G2's built-in microphone to issue complex commands, like "Computer, open my last downloaded PDF and email it to Sarah," or "Play my lofi playlist on Spotify." The agent on your computer executes the clicks and keystrokes, and you get a real-time status update floating in your heads-up display. It's a hands-free, AI-powered remote control for your desktop, and the possibilities are limitless. Just be warned that installing any agentic AI program on your computer leaves you vulnerable to attack via prompt injection. Try this one only if you understand the risks.

You don't have to be a birder to want to know what's making that racket in the tree above you. Birdie, a lightweight Even Hub app from a solo developer, listens to bird sounds through your G2's mic and identifies bird species using BirdNET—the same open-source bird-sound recognition model used by "serious" birding tools. Start a listening pass, hold still a few seconds, and when it gets a confident match, the species' common name, scientific name, and a field-guide photo pop up on your HUD. It's not doing anything a bird-identifying phone app like Merlin couldn't do, but it does it better. Since it listens in the background, you don't have to whip out your phone and point it at a branch when you see a grackle; instead, you just get your bird information fed directly into your eyeballs.

A lot of people are up in arms over facial recognition software being added to Meta glasses, but how about voice recognition? What's Their Face is an app on the Even Hub that uses voice recognition to act as a digital Rolodex for your acquaintances, aiming to solve the dreaded "cocktail party problem" of "what is their name??"

It works like this: You record a five-second clip of a person speaking and attach it to a name and an information card that can contain job titles, email addresses, or anything else you want. A few days later, when you run into that person and you've forgotten their name, your glasses will flash the closest matching voice prints so you can pretend you knew all along. If you have privacy concerns, this is a memory aid, not a privacy invasion tool. All the computation is done on the device, and no information is pulled from online sources and connected to a person you meet—you can only enter what you know about a person. No information is sent anywhere either, so it can't create a universal database of names so you'd "recognize" people you haven't met.

When I first got G1 Even Reality glasses, I immediately used them to trick a bartender out of a drink by offering to answer any trivia question, then correctly naming FW Murnau's follow-up film to 1927's Sunrise. (My glasses tell me it's 4 Devils, released in 1928.) This kind of mild flim-flammery is even easier with the second generation, thanks to Conversate, G2's always-listening mode that quietly transcribes conversation and surfaces context in real time. You can use this easily to convince people you are a math wiz, or you know the day of the week they were born based on the date, or that you have memorized the name, number, and position of everyone who has ever played for the Cleveland Browns.

Like most magic tricks, the mechanics are simple: turn on Conversate and let it listen for a question and feed you an answer only you will see, although you might have to repeat the question if Conversate's AI doesn't "pick it up" when it's first said. The hack here is really the performance: being able to repeat a question back and make it sound natural, reading the screen without looking like you're reading the screen, dealing with any "pauses" in the AI by realistically looking like you're thinking, then waiting a beat to make the answer seem natural. If you decide you like jovially deceiving people and you want to make it your career, check out sybil sight, a "mentalism operating system" for Even Realities G2 glasses. It's not cheap, and they don't tell you how it works exactly because a magician's secrets are only unlocked with cash, but I'm picturing a way more elaborate version of the tricks described above.

The great thing about G2 glasses is how many very specific problems they solve, like making sure your band knows what chord to play when. Here's how to never have to say, "OK, the next chord is E minor" again so you can just rock out:

Get a pair of G2 glasses for everyone in the group. (Yeah, it's a high bar to clear.)

Have everyone download QMe Prompter and install it on their phones.

Have everyone set the app to stream content directly to G2 glasses.

Use the app's "group jam" feature to link everyone over wifi. When the leader pulls up a chord chart, it instantly loads lyrics and chords onto everyone's phones, which beams it to their spectacles.

The app has hands-free scrolling that can be set by BPM, a foot pedal, or you can use the voice-follow feature that listens to the singer and scrolls the lyrics in time, so everyone is on the same page.

Pro-tip: Your band probably needs the Even Hub's Tuner app too.

title: Spotify Just Launched a New Running Mode, and I'm Surprised How Much I Love It
description: The kick drum got me to maintain every runner's dream: exactly 180bpm.
fullText:
I'm currently training for a marathon this fall, and today was supposed to be a rest day. Spotify had other plans for me: Today the company launched a new running mode, so I laced up and put it to the test.

This new mode cues up songs based on the different phases of your run and selects tracks based on your preferences and desired tempo. Instead of just shuffling a playlist and hoping the BPM lines up with your cadence, it builds a run around your effort structure: warmup, work intervals, recovery, cooldown. On top of the music, it layers in audio cues at key moments of the run, so you're getting something closer to a coached session, like Nike Run Club is known for.

Only paid subscribers can currently access this new running mode. Search "fitness" in the app to pull up what it calls the "Fitness Hub," and running mode is right at the top. From there, you can choose from one of 25 presets, or build your own from scratch.

Once you're in running mode, you first pick a workout type: Just Run, Easy Runs, Interval, Pyramid, or Long and Advanced. Then you choose a music genre. For me, the options were pop, hip-hop, EDM, rock, and R&B.

I messed around with a few presets before landing on the one I actually wanted to test properly: a Pyramid Rock Run. Here's how I "refined" it:

Bumped the duration from 30 to 35 minutes.

Workout type: I chose pyramid, which comes with a helpful graphic showing what the effort structure looks like over the course of the run.

More genre options showed up at this stage, including house, Latin, classical, and country. There's also a "discovery slider," so I pushed mine to 75% toward new music.

Toggled on using a target BPM for song selection, set it to 180, and also turned on "adjust song speed to match exactly," though after my test run, I'm not sure what this was supposed to do exactly.

After I locked in those settings, it took Spotify a solid two minutes to generate the playlist. Once it's built, you get options to smart reorder, add tracks, or refine further. Two things I noticed right away: It nailed the 75% new music request (fun!); the run started at 133 bpm (solid), climbed to a peak of 180 (perfect), and then the cooldown had one track sitting at 210 bpm (confusing and bad).

I thoroughly enjoyed my test run with this new feature today, even though I was supposed to be resting. Beyond the novelty, I think this is a genuinely good tool for runners trying to sharpen their internal sense of pace. Locking music tempo to target cadence gives you something to run alongside, and effort structures like pyramids force you to notice how your stride changes as intensity shifts. The audio coaching reminded me of what I've always liked about Nike Run Club: form cues and, more often than not, reminders to slow down, which is advice most runners need more than they know.

Spotify's AI coach delivers that guidance by way of music, always announcing each song, which I enjoyed. For instance, during the hip-hop playlist, one cue told me to "let the groove loosen my stride, and remember to unclench your fists and drop your shoulders." On the rock playlist, during a peak effort segment, it told me to "keep it snappy, but not forced." My pitch to Spotify here would be to announce the song's bpm, too.

One note worth remembering: the coach isn't actually responding to you in real time—it's all pre-set according to your workout preferences. Still, I approve of these built-in settings. The only real miss was that 210 bpm cooldown track. Everything else about the pacing logic tracked, which made that one outlier stand out more.

My favorite piece of coaching advice was to lock into the kick drum. I tried it during "Misery Business" by Paramore, and according to my Garmin Forerunner 970, I was running at exactly 180 bpm. Even if runners don't love the songs that Spotify selected for them (although I had no complaints personally), I'd still recommend this feature as a fun way to perfect your inner metronome and practice pacing before race day.

title: Here's What Lifehacker Readers Think Apple Will Announce in the Fall
description: These are the results of the second round of Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game.
fullText:
Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game finished its second round last week. The game invites readers to make predictions on what products and features Apple may announce this year, all for the chance to win the latest Apple Watch. While we won't know the answers of these questions until Apple's September event, we do have the results. Check out what Lifehacker readers think Apple will announce this year, and come back Aug. 18 to participate in the final round.

Apple is almost assuredly going to reveal its first foldable iPhone during WWDC this year. The major question left is, what will the company call it? Lifehacker asked readers to pick from the following four options: iPhone 18 Fold, iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra, or none of the above. While iPhone Ultra was the most popular name choice, with 30% of readers choosing it, slightly more respondents think Apple will go with another name. We'll see who is right in just over a month.

Apple devices are notoriously expensive, and those prices are only continuing to rise. As such, it stands to reason that Apple's most complex and feature-filled iPhone yet will also be its priciest. Nearly a quarter of Lifehacker respondents believe the price will be somewhere between $1,000 and $1,499, while another near quarter think it'll cost $1,500 to $1,999. However, a whopping 41% believe it will cost more than $2,000. Personally, I think that's a good guess, considering the product and the current state of the market.

The iPhone 18 Pro will likely take a backseat to Apple's foldable iPhone, and, as such, will likely be a small upgrade over the iPhone 17 Pro. Still, rumors speculate that Apple will shrink the size of the Dynamic Island on the 18 Pro, to make it a bit less pronounced when looking at the display. A little less than 43% of respondents don't buy that, while just over 57% believe it. While it'd be great to get as close to no camera cutout as possible, for a truly screen-only iPhone front, I find the Dynamic Island useful, and I'm not sure making it smaller would improve that.

While the Apple Watch Series 11 can detect wrist temperature, Apple is also upgrading the health sensors on its wearables. As such, it's possible the next generation of Apple Waches could read your body temperature as a whole, replacing the need for dedicated thermometers. While nearly 18% don't think that's coming, over 82% do.

One AirPods rumor that has persisted for years is that Apple is working on embedding cameras in its earbuds. While that might sound ridiculous, the concept actually makes sense: Apple would use these cameras not to take pictures, but to allow Siri AI to see the world around you. It could turn your AirPods into an AI device, and eliminate the need for you to take out your iPhone every time you want to ask the assistant a visual question. That said, most Lifehacker readers don't think Apple will do this, including over 68% of respondents. We'll just have to see what Apple decides to do.

title: Study suggests the threat of mold-associated illnesses may be underappreciated
description: A first-of-its-kind U.S. study suggests invasive mold infections may be an underappreciated — and potentially deadly — threat.  The findings, published this week by the U.S.
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — A first-of-its-kind U.S. study suggests invasive mold infections may be an underappreciated — and potentially deadly — threat.

The researchers detected about 450 cases in Atlanta-area hospitals over five years. About a third of the patients died in the hospital.

The findings, published this week by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, come from an attempt to better gauge how common these kinds of illnesses are. The government does not require doctors to report the illnesses.

"It's kind of the first time we've had an estimate like this," said the CDC's Dr. Jeremy Gold, the study's senior author.

And it's important to understand it now, because the problem may grow in the future, he added. Mold exposure is a recurring problem in the wake of hurricanes, floods and other natural disasters influenced by climate change, researchers have found.

"I agree that the frequency of fungal infections will likely increase with climate change," said Dr. Jeffrey Jenks, an infectious disease researcher at Duke University.

Meanwhile, there's a growing population of older people who are more susceptible to such illnesses, Gold said.

Invasive mold diseases are rare infections caused by certain species. Most people who get infected inhale mold spores, but they can also enter the body through cuts or wounds or from contaminated medical equipment.

The spores don't cause health problems for most people, but they can be life-threatening to some, including the elderly, cancer patients and others with weakened immune systems.

Previously, CDC researchers estimated more than 15,000 hospitalizations a year could be tied to invasive mold disease.

To better understand how common cases might be at a local level, the research team worked with four Atlanta-area hospitals and their affiliated outpatient clinics to look for potential cases from 2020 to 2024.

They initially identified nearly 1,000 potential cases, but winnowed the number down to about 450 by ruling out patients who may have had signs of exposure but didn't qualify as having invasive mold disease.

The researchers found that hospitals can expect to see 3 to 5 cases per year for every 100 inpatient beds. The rates were higher at larger academic hospitals that tend to see more complicated illnesses.

Most patients had impaired immune systems or — in a number of cases — were weakened after falling sick from COVID-19.

Mold exposures can occur in hospitals or other healthcare facilities, but the study did not try to determine where each patient was first exposed, Gold said.

It's hard to generalize what was seen in the Atlanta area to other parts of the country where mold may be more or less of a problem, he said. But it should give hospital administrators at least a rough idea about whether the number of cases they see is what might be expected or whether it's an outbreak, Gold added.

Jenks called the study's findings "valuable," but said "seeing results from similar studies done in different parts of the United States would be helpful."

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.

title: Red state governor pummeled online after defying Trump’s deportation orders
description: Gov. Mike DeWine called Haiti "hell" while arguing against deporting Haitian TPS holders, sparking fierce online backlash from critics on social media.
fullText:
A Republican governor in a state that voted to elect President Donald Trump is facing intense backlash online after an interview arguing against the president's order to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) migrants from the United States.

Republican Gov. Mike DeWine's state is home to an estimated 30,000 Haitian TPS holders. He told CBS earlier this week that the Haitians shouldn't be sent back to their country of origin.

"Haiti is hell today. So you'd be sending people… back to hell," he said. "Very few of these Haitians will voluntarily go back to Haiti. If they have to leave, they'll go someplace else. They want to work. They want to support their family. They don't want to go back to Haiti."

Blue State Leaders Erupt After Supreme Court's Decision Ending Tps Protections For Haitians, Syrians

Online detractors quickly seized on DeWine's comments, mostly from users claiming that those responsible for Haiti's conditions are the ones that the governor wants to allow to stay in the United States.

"What makes Haiti hellish? Is it… the Haitians?" asked Sean Davis, co-founder of The Federalist, in response to CBS' story about the interview posted on X.

"Hey governor, what is it that makes Haiti so bad anyway?" The Blaze's Logan Hall asked.

"I think the real question here is, if Haiti is hell, why are we importing Haitians?" questioned internet personality Larry Sanger.

Trump's 'Third World' Travel Ban Could Become Permanent If Firebrand Republican Lawmaker Gets Her Way

Others referenced the liberal media's freakout when, in 2018, Trump referred to Haiti and some other nations as "s---hole" countries.

Meanwhile, TV personalities and talking heads, comedian Conan O'Brien chief among them, defended Haiti for its natural beauty.

"Still reeling from [Trump's] very negative Yelp review of Haiti, which means I'll love it," O'Brien said at the time, announcing a trip to the country. "I have no idea what the president has against the people of Haiti, but if the president doesn't like them, they must be lovely people."

Dem-led Push To Extend Protections For Haitians Faces Outrage After Brutal Hammer Killing

One X user specifically blamed Haitians for DeWine's characterization that the country is "hell."

"Or is it a paradise like so many celebrities have said?" the user asked.

"I was reliably informed by democrats [sic] and hollywood [sic] celebrities that Haiti is utopia," said another user.

"What a tragedy it would be for Haitians to live in Haiti," said another X user.

DeWine argued in the CBS interview that sending Haitians back to Haiti would be a "mistake" that would endanger the lives of the TPS holders.

He also specifically mentioned Springfield, his hometown, which has a large population of Haitian TPS holders.

"These are people who have helped Springfield really come back," DeWine said. "The Haitians who are living there and employed there, they came there to work, and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people."

TPS was officially terminated Monday after Trump's order survived a Supreme Court review.

"Temporary Protected Status is exactly that — temporary. For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent," a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Fox News Digital earlier this week.

TPS was created as part of the Immigration Act of 1990, and was designed for people facing serious emergencies like armed conflict or severe natural disasters. Critics claim it has been abused to give status to those in the U.S. for non-emergent reasons.

DeWine's office declined to comment on "statements made in online comment sections," when reached by Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.

Fox News Digital's Andrew Mark Miller contributed to this report.

title: 'Nothing to prove' at Commonwealths for Finucane
description: Olympic team sprint champion Emma Finucane insists she has nothing to prove in Glasgow as she chases a Commonwealth gold medal.
fullText:
Olympic champion cyclist Emma Finucane insists she has "nothing to prove" at the Commonwealth Games despite her ambitions of winning an elusive gold in Scotland.

Finucane, 23, collected two bronze medals in Birmingham four years ago but has since won 16 medals at the Olympics, World and European Championships.

The Welsh star says she is targeting "the top step" on the podium in Glasgow.

"I haven't actually stood on the top step at the Commonwealth Games," Finucane told BBC Sport Wales.

"That's something I'd love to achieve this time round.

"I feel like I'm a different person four years on and I can't wait to show what I can do on the track."

The Carmarthenshire native credits the Birmingham 2022 Games as the "springboard" to where she is today.

"I would not be where I am today without the Commonwealth Games," she said.

"The first time I was pretty young, pretty naive to the sport of sprint cycling.

"It was a very overwhelming experience, whereas this time round I feel like I'm more of an established rider."

She added: "I was 19 [in Birmingham] and the year after I won my first world title, which was crazy for me.

"I think it gave me the confidence I needed as an athlete to develop in my career, and get to where I am so quickly.

"We became Olympic champions two years ago, and I actually don't even know how that happened."

Finucane will compete in the team sprint, the individual sprint, the 1km time trial and the keirin in Glasgow.

There is an impressive crop of British track cycling sprinters threatening her ambitions at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

The England team has Finucane's Olympic gold-winning team-mates Sophie Capewell and Katy Marchant, while Rhianna Parris-Smith has helped Finucane to UCI Track World Cup silver in Hong Kong this year.

Scotland's Lauren Bell, who won sprint and keirin gold at the British Championships in 2024, could also provide stiff competition.

And that's before mentioning New Zealand's Ellesse Andrews, who won three golds in Birmingham in the individual sprint, keirin and team sprint competitions.

Wales at the Commonwealth Games

Finucane's partner, Matt Richardson is also a cyclist and represents England after switching allegiance from Australia.

She says they have a "fun relationship on the bike".

"We are really competitive people; if it's a game of Monopoly or it's a bike race, we are competitive and I think we use that to our strength.

Finucane says dating a fellow cyclist helps them to get what the other person might need, whether competitions have gone well or badly.

"He understands completely what I'm feeling or how the times are, what I'll be happy with or what I'll be disappointed with.

"That's something really nice and not many people get that.

"You can literally go to your partner and he'll be like 'It's okay'.

"He gives me so much advice on what I can do or how to deal with things and I'd like to say vice versa.

"He's a lot more experienced than me, but I think I do bring a presence of a bit more calm and maybe perspective in the sport too.

"I think we're a good team together."

Richardson however will no longer be competing at the Games after being forced out by injury.

Welsh rider Finucane sets new world sprint record

Finucane makes history with third medal in Paris

Finucane wants to be 'unstoppable' by 2028 Olympics

Finucane hopes a good showing in Glasgow will enhance her legacy in the sport.

"For us there's pressure everywhere, but I also feel calm coming into this Commonwealth Games; I have nothing to prove," she said.

"Obviously I do want to stand on that top step, and that will be the goal I'm trying to do; I've never achieved that in my career.

"But also I have my 'Oscars', as I call them.

"I won the Olympics, I've become world champion and I want to see how far I've gone in this sport.

"I want to win as much as I can, I want to be on the track as much as I can, representing Team Wales.

"So there is pressure. I'll definitely use that to drive me to try to win as many bike races as I can.

"It'll be insane to be in Glasgow, wearing the Welsh jersey, in front of my friends and family.

"I'm going to see how far I can go."

title: Scotland win eight medals in five chaotic hours as Games hit halfway
description: Host nation Scotland win eight medals in the space of five chaotic hours on Wednesday - two of them gold - to take their Commonwealth Games tally in Glasgow to 23.
fullText:
Host nation Scotland won eight medals in the space of five chaotic hours on Wednesday - two of them gold - to take their Commonwealth Games tally in Glasgow to 23.

Swimmers Angharad Evans and Keanna MacInnes both won an individual medal and a relay prize, and Toni Shaw also tasted success in the pool at Tollcross.

Melanie Woods roared to gold on the track at Scotstoun, before Steven MacKenzie earned a surprise bronze in the field.

And at the SEC, both the men's 3x3 basketball team and their women's wheelchair equivalents ended the evening on the podium.

It takes Scotland's tally to 23 overall as the Games passes the halfway mark - nine gold and seven of both silver and bronze.

And it is the best return in a single day since nine were claimed on the last day of the Birmingham edition in 2022.

Woods sets Games record to claim gold for Scotland

No car park tears this time for Love as 3x3 teams claim silver & bronze

After a relatively quiet day, the first medal was claimed by the men's 3x3 basketball team just before 17:00 BST.

A couple of hours later, three more followed in the space of five minutes.

The women's wheelchair 3x3 basketball team took silver; Evans added her second gold - and third medal - of the Games in the 200m breaststroke; then Woods claimed gold in the women's T54 1500m.

Shaw then joined in with bronze in the women's S9 100m freestyle before MacInnes was edged into second place in the women's 200m butterfly to take her second individual silver of the meet.

Around the same time, MacKenzie was leaping to long jump bronze, before the haul was completed in the pool when Evans and MacInnes teamed up with Katie Shanahan and Evie Davis to take silver in the women's 4x100m medley.

Three more further medals are guaranteed in boxing - with fighters in semi-final action on Friday - while further prospects remain in athletics, bowls, cycling, judo and weightlifting.

title: No car park tears this time for Love as 3x3 teams claim silver & bronze
description: After tears in Birmingham four years ago, Robyn Love gets on to the podium at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
Four years ago, in a converted car park in Birmingham, tears fell down Robyn Love's cheeks and thumping music assaulted her ears.

A Commonwealth Games that started with a lost chair had ended in a missed opportunity for Scotland's women's wheelchair 3x3 basketball team.

A bronze medal had been lost to hosts England amid the rambunctious surroundings of Smithfield Market, and Love was trying to explain how much it hurt when her emotions took over.

Fast forward four years and the 35-year-old from Ayr was the sole survivor from that team as Scotland faced England again on Wednesday in Glasgow.

The difference this time was that it was in the gold-medal match.

Love, Lea Smith, Kayli English and Jodie Waite knew they would leave the SEC with - at worst - a slab of silver around their necks after beating Australia in the semi-final earlier in the day. And ultimately that's what happened after an 18-10 defeat.

That they - officially at least - missed out on becoming Scotland's first ever Commonwealth medallists in a team sport after being usurped by their men's 3x3 pals winning bronze earlier in the day will not have concerned them in the slightest.

"I'm not crying now, but I pretty much was this morning after the semi-final," said veteran Love, who also coaches this callow team.

"To get a Commonwealth silver with this group, and to get to coach them and see them grow... what a privilege. I feel incredibly lucky and it's much better being in the SEC than in a car park in Birmingham, I can tell you that for free."

Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final

The 23-year-old teacher leading lesson on stripping bowls' stigma

All the latest from Team Scotland at the Games

Two of the men's team are no strangers to Games pain either.

Kyle Jimenez and Ross Malcolm lost in the bronze-medal game to New Zealand in Gold Coast in 2018, and again four years later against Canada.

They were not going to let their opportunity pass a third time.

New Zealand - who had beaten them in the round robin - were the opposition again, but the Scottish-born duo - and US-raised team-mates Skylar White and Owen McCormack - kept their shape in an angst-ridden contest to win 18-16.

"We needed to keep it interesting for you guys," White, whose father is from Kilmarnock, told fans afterwards.

He added: "Towards the end, I told the guys 'you can be hurt tomorrow, you can feel sore tomorrow, but right now it's time to nut up and get it done'."

McCormack, who qualifies through his Scottish mother, said the feeling of taking bronze ranked among the "top two... and it's not two" in his life.

He also paid tribute to Malcolm and Jimenez, who have long been passionate advocates for the sport in Scotland as well as elite performers.

And that duo spoke movingly about what this success could mean in a wider sense.

"Coming into this we all believed we could get a medal as a team, but no one else thought anything of us - we proved the world wrong today," Jimenez said.

Malcolm added: "Every time we play on an international stage we punch above our weight. Hopefully we get the coverage and the publicity that the sport deserves."

Amid the joy, though, there was disappointment for the wheelchair men's team, who lost their bronze-medal match to Canada 19-9.

title: From bad to worse for Trump and his base
description: Republicans are starting to fret about their base’s lack of enthusiasm ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
fullText:
Republicans are starting to fret about their base's lack of enthusiasm ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

Those voters were already disproportionately less likely to vote in elections not featuring Donald Trump, and now the GOP has to contend with the president being more unpopular than ever.

And a new CNN poll drives home the problem: Large portions of Trump's base are feeling disillusioned over more than a few of his choices lately.

Across a bevy of questions — on subjects ranging from the economy to the Iran war to Trump's self-enrichment and efforts to makeover Washington — large percentages of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents are registering discontent. As in, often 30%, 40%, 50% or more.

Overall, the CNN poll shows 30% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents disapprove of Trump.

That number is rather high in and of itself. But it actually might undersell the level of disillusionment on some fronts.

Without question, the most troubling numbers for Trump and the GOP concern the economy.

Not only is the economy generally voters' biggest concern; it also features Trump's worst numbers.

To wit, among Republicans and GOP-leaning independents in the poll:

64% say high gas prices have caused at least a "moderate" hardship for them

56% say the economy is very or somewhat poor

56% say Trump hasn't gone far enough to reduce the price of everyday goods

56% disapprove of Trump's performance on gas prices

51% say Trump doesn't have a clear plan on gas prices

50% say Trump's policies haven't improved economic conditions (with 31% saying his policies have actually made things worse)

47% disapprove of Trump on inflation

That's around half or more of what should be Trump's own supporters that have a lot of gripes about the economy and his handling of it right now.

The numbers are slightly less grim on Iran, but still pretty grim.

Again, among Republicans and GOP-leaning independents:

64% think a long-term war with Iran is likely

45% say the toll of the war — in lives and money — hasn't been worth it

45% say Trump doesn't have a clear plan for Iran

40% disapprove of Trump overall on Iran

39% say his decisions about military action in Iran have hurt the US (versus 44% who say it has helped, with the rest being neutral)

And Trump's trend line on Iran continues to be bad. Trump's disapproval on Iran among these groups has increased from 30% in March to 40% today.

The poll also shows many members of Trump's base simply don't like what he's focused on — including his personal finances and projects like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

45% say Trump isn't "in touch with the problems ordinary Americans face in their daily lives" — up from 34% in January

39% say he hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems — up from 25% in January

Around 3 in 10 say he's "gone too far" in changing institutions like the Smithsonian and the Kennedy Center (which Trump put his name on before a judge removed it), remodeling the White House and other Washington landmarks and pursuing personal business interests while in the White House

30% say Trump doesn't put the good of the country over his personal gain

26% say they're angry or dissatisfied about the ballroom and the reflecting pool (compared to just 39% who are positive about these projects)

It would be bad enough for Trump if the economy were suboptimal and people didn't think the things he did were working.

But these numbers — combined with the majority of Trump's base that says he's neglected inflation — make clear many of his backers think he's preoccupied with things that either aren't worth focusing on or are actively unpopular.

When many of these questions were asked in Trump's first months back in office, there was a palpable sense of enthusiasm with his base.

When asked to describe their feelings looking ahead to the rest of Trump's second term, nearly nine in 10 of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents said they were "enthusiastic" or "optimistic."

Now, that number has dropped all the way to 70%.

And 30% say they're either "pessimistic" or "afraid."

That 30% who have a negative outlook is pretty remarkable. Shortly after former President Barack Obama was reelected in 2012, just 8% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they felt pessimistic or afraid. And just before former President George W. Bush's reelection in 2004, only 5% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents said the same about him.

Then there's the findings of a recent Pew Research Center poll.

That poll showed 81% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said their midterm vote would be a vote against Trump, compared to just 44% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents who said theirs would be a vote for Trump.

There have been signs of this kind of malaise dating back a year, when the Jeffrey Epstein saga exploded. The latest numbers suggest it's now taken hold in large swaths of the GOP base — at a very inopportune time for the party.

title: Laura Ingraham stands at Fauci hearing alongside others ‘shamed’ during COVID-19
description: Fox News host Laura Ingraham was on hand to watch Dr. Anthony Fauci answer questions at Wednesday’s Senate hearing, sitting behind him and standing up when Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) asked about peop...
fullText:
Fox News host Laura Ingraham was on hand to watch Dr. Anthony Fauci answer questions at Wednesday's Senate hearing, sitting behind him and standing up when Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) asked about people being "shamed" during the COVID-19 pandemic.

When Moreno requested people in the audience stand up if they had controversial beliefs or actions surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic and may have faced backlash for those beliefs or actions, Ingraham stood.

"All you have to do is look up from your lawyers and look at the people who were absolutely shamed for saying what we know now to be the truth," Moreno told Fauci during the hearing.

Ingraham, as the COVID-19 pandemic was raging in the U.S., criticized the use of coronavirus vaccines and said that Americans should not have to receive them.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, conservatives often raged against public health measures and advice meant to protect against the virus, including masking and vaccinations.

Fauci, the former chief White House medical adviser, invoked his Fifth Amendment right at a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on Wednesday held by the committee's chair, Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.).

Fauci went after Paul's "obvious obsession" with calling for the health official's prosecution. Fauci and Paul have a history of tension during congressional hearings.

"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Resurfaced video shows James Talarico discussing ‘exciting’ opportunity to end ‘over-policing’
description: Resurfaced video shows James Talarico calling efforts to end over-policing "really exciting" after 2020 Black Lives Matter riots in Austin, Texas.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: A resurfaced video shows that following the 2020 Black Lives Matter riots in the wake of George Floyd's death, now-Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico said the country was facing a "really exciting" opportunity to "end the current situation of over-policing communities of color which has been in place in this country since its founding."

Talarico, a Texas state lawmaker, is tied in recent polling with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the race to be the state's next U.S. senator. Such a flip would be the first in decades and would deal a major blow to the GOP's chances of retaining a Senate majority. Despite a history of controversial statements, including calling God nonbinary and claiming there are six genders, Talarico has recently positioned himself as a moderate, pro-police candidate.

However, critics are calling his pro-police stance into question after they say the resurfaced video destroys that narrative.

Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, ripped Talarico as a "dangerous freak who is willing to endanger the entire state just to prove that he is sufficiently woke."

Far-left Senate Hopeful Explains 'Ogre On A Pike' Remark After Getting Torched By His Own Party

Kraft alleged that "James Talarico's wacked out vision for Texas with no police, no prisons, and no borders would put families in danger and be a paradise for criminal illegal aliens."

Unearthed clips from a September 2020 Zoom with South Asian American Voter Empowerment (SAAVETX) show Talarico saying that policymakers need to "listen to black voices and to the activists in the streets calling for a radically different vision of public safety."

He ripped Republicans who he accused of wanting to "scare white people to win an election," saying that "is a time-honored tradition in the Republican Party."

Talarico asserted that "police violence against communities of color, in particular our black community is nothing new, and has its roots in slavery and Jim Crow and mass incarceration."

He added that "this is just the latest iteration of the history of oppression this country has been a part of against African Americans."

Meanwhile, he said he would like to gather people "from activists and advocates to community leaders to law enforcement officials themselves to have a genuine discussion about what true public safety policy looks like and how we can end the current situation of over-policing communities of color which has been in place in this country since its founding."

He added that the discussion should be about "how do we take our criminal justice system at the state level, at the national level, and how do we make some fundamental changes to reflect our highest ideals and to really embody the country and state and the community that we want in the race to be."

"That's taking place," he continued, adding that communities are "figuring out how we reinvest our limited public funding into these community-based solutions that really start to address the underlying causes of our criminal justice system attempts to treat."

"That to me is really exciting," he said.

Dsa Co-chair Embraces Abolishing Senate, Ice, Borders As Democratic Infighting Escalates

Talarico proceeded to say, "I applaud our local leaders that are trying to do that." He cited the city of Austin, which had recently approved a budget that cut tens of millions of dollars from the Austin Police Department. He ripped Republican Gov. Greg Abbott for having "proposed removing some of the revenue streams from cities like Austin because they've made local decisions for their local community."

At the time, Abbott released a statement saying that "Austin's decision puts the brave men and women of the Austin Police Department and their families at greater risk, and paves the way for lawlessness." The governor promised financial penalties for any Texas city defunding its police force, saying, "Public safety is job one, and Austin has abandoned that duty."

During the Zoom call, however, Talarico asserted that for Abbott to "complain about local communities not funding public safety is hypocritical."

"To see the governor continue to try to undermine our local governments, I think is rich to say the least," he said.

In response to the new criticism, JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico's campaign, told Fox News Digital that "James opposes defunding the police, has voted to deny bail for violent criminals, and has a record of sending billions of dollars to support law enforcement."

Additionally, Ennis said that Talarico "supports a secure southern border and has unveiled a border security agenda backed by law enforcement officials from both parties."

Meanwhile, he accused Paxton of having "abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected, allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe," adding, "Even Ken Paxton's fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free."

Maine's New Democratic Senate Nominee, Troy Jackson, Tells Fox News Digital 'I've Been Vetted'

Ennis has previously called the assertion that Talarico is pro-defund the police a "flat out lie."

He said that previous legislation proposed by Talarico "supports the police by adding desperately needed mental health officials to help prevent tragic events like the mass shooting at Robb Elementary in Uvalde, Texas."

Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for Paxton's campaign, said that "James Talarico has the most consistently anti-law enforcement record in the Texas Legislature. But now his spokesman is out telling bold-faced lies."

"For his campaign to even insinuate that Talarico has, at any point in his career, 'stood with law enforcement' is one of the most egregious lies they have told throughout this campaign," Cercy told Fox News Digital.

She said that Talarico "donated thousands of dollars to an organization that supported defunding the police and voted against banning personal bond release for people accused of violent crimes," while emphasizing that "just because he votes on a basic spending bill like every other state representative does not mean he has ever 'supported law enforcement.'"

"If it were up to Talarico," she continued, "We would hand over our communities to the radicals who pillaged our streets during the 2020 defund the police movement and let criminals out of prison in pursuit of a socialist agenda."

Fox News Digital reached out to SAAVETX for comment.

title: Pretorius drives Spirit to win over MI London
description: Lhuan-dre Pretorius recovers from a heavy collision in the field to hit 64 as London Spirit beat MI London by seven wickets for their first win in this season's Hundred.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, The Oval

MI London 164-5 (100 balls): Jacks 65 (44); Overton 3-30

London Spirit 165-3 (89 balls): Pretorius 64 (28); Gleeson 1-23

London Spirit won by seven wickets

Lhuan-dre Pretorius recovered from a heavy collision in the field to hit 64 as London Spirit beat MI London by seven wickets for their first win in this season's Hundred.

The South African and James Coles ran into one another chasing a catch late in the first innings, in which reach MI London reached 164-5.

Pretorius left the field after the incident but was fit to open the Spirit innings and hit three fours and seven sixes in his 28-ball innings, which started with a 63-run partnership with Jonny Bairstow (23).

The 20-year-old added a further 38 with Liam Livingstone (16) before he was caught by Sherfane Rutherford off the bowling of Richard Gleeson.

James Rew (19) and Dewald Brevis (37 from 18) finished the job off for Spirit, who won with 11 balls to spare.

MI London had started well after being put into bat, with Will Jacks (65) and James Vince (26) putting on a 91-run opening partnership.

However both openers and Nicholas Pooran fell in the space of eight balls as the home side slipped to 100-3.

Both Jacks and Pooran were dismissed by Jamie Overton, who later removed Jason Roy (13) for figures of 3-30.

Rutherford accelerated at the close for MI, striking a 19-ball 41 that featured four sixes before he was caught by Coles off Andrew Tye from the last ball of the innings.

Spirit move into sixth, above Southern Brave and Birmingham Phoenix, after claiming their first win in three matches, while MI London sit in fourth with two wins and two defeats.

Who am I? Guess The Hundred cricket star No 9

Southern Brave face Birmingham Phoenix in Southampton on Thursday.

In the women's competition, the home side, who sit at the top of the table, will be aiming for a fourth win from as many matches, while Phoenix are yet to win after two games. They meet at 15:00 BST.

Brave's men, meanwhile, will be eyeing their first win of the season in the match that follows at 18.30.

You can follow ball-by-ball commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

title: Evans battles nerves to become Scotland's breakout star
description: Angharad Evans added another breaststroke gold to become Scotland's breakout star in the pool at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
Angharad Evans describes herself as a "nervous swimmer" who dare not even let herself think of getting a medal. She ended the Commonwealth Games swimming meet as Scotland's breakout star.

Double breaststroke gold, and a relay bronze and silver means her strategy of keeping expectations low must work. But after an imperious performance across the week at a raucous Tollcross, they will never be as low again.

After recovering from a slow start, Evans powered to 200m breaststroke gold to add to her first place in the 100m on the final night of swimming action, during which Scotland claimed four medals.

A couple of hours later Evans' superb second leg helped Scotland into silver medal position behind Australia in the women's 4x100m medley relay - her fourth medal of these home games.

Only one of her training partners at Stirling University, Duncan Scott no less, tipped her for big things in Glasgow. Even Evans did not believe.

"It's been a big step forward in my career," Evans told BBC Scotland.

"There are things I've battled with this week. I don't hide from my nerves - it's something I'm very open about.

"I'm a very nervous swimmer but I proved to myself that even though I am nervous I can get medals individually and in relays, even when I'm tired on the last day.

"But it makes it a lot easier doing in front of a crowd like that and with your team-mates you train with every day."

Scotland win eight medals in five chaotic hours as Games hit halfway

Woods sets Games record to claim gold for Scotland

Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final

Evans, like many of her team-mates, has memories to cherish from these Glasgow Games. After her 200m gold she looked almost stunned as the crowd went nuts around her.

Evans emerged from the water and tried to take it all in. Her family and boyfriend were scattered around the small arena, but she managed to spot them all and get hugs. There was even a guard of honour with team-mates bedecked in kilts.

It was all so far from what Evans had allowed herself to dream of.

"I disassociate the idea of getting a medal because that's when I operate best," the Cambridge-born athlete said.

"It was a very special moment for me. Going into the Commonwealth Games with no expectations and coming out with two gold medals and a bronze [and silver] in the relay has just been so surreal.

"It just shows the hard work that we've been doing in Stirling."

So, can this be the springboard for more?

"Right now it's just taking a breath and taking it in before we hit Europeans [Championships next week]. We'll see what happens there.

"But as I said, I think this is a really big step forward for me - and hopefully the Europeans will be another step forward. I won't go out without a fight."

Evans steps out of shadows into spotlight with Scotland's fourth gold

A Scottish gold made up for the fact Scott missed out on his bid to defend his 200m freestyle title and add a 16th Commonwealth medal, having failed to qualify for the final at the end of a rigorous schedule.

And Evans' success was not the only one cheered to the roof of Tollcross instead.

Aberdeen's Toni Shaw stopped an Australian clean sweep of medals in the women's S9 100m freestlye final to replicate the bronze of Birmingham four years ago.

"I had lots and lots of nerves even before the walkout, all day since my heat," Shaw told BBC Scotland.

"But we've got a good support team and they helped me keep my cool and wish me luck. All you can do is swim as fast as you can and that's the mentality I went into the race with."

Meanwhile, Keanna MacInnes added 200m butterfly silver, having also come second in the 100m. The 24-year-old played her part in the relay silver too to take her own tally to three.

As she stood next to her relay team-mates Katie Shanahan, Evans, and Evelyn Davis the Stirling swimmer reflected on a Games during which Scottish swimmers have delivered 12 medals, four of them gold.

"If you said to me at the start of the week I'd win two medals I'd be over the moon - sneaking that extra mixed medley one last night was special for all of us," MacInnes said.

"We heard it a 100 times, about the crowd being amazing but it absolutely delivered. I'm a proud and patriotic Scot so there's been a lot of tears this week.

"Not only is it 12 medals but there are a lot of golds and silvers, not necessarily sneaking into bronze. That shows the depth.

"There were so many finals with multiple Scots in them. So not just medals but lots of personal and season's bests which shows how good the team has been this week."

title: 'Change is inevitable' - Liverpool CEO on FSG, Iraola and consortium talks
description: Liverpool Billy Hogan talks to BBC Sport in New York about investment, transition and why FSG aren't done yet.
fullText:
With Liverpool stating that they have more than 26 million supporters in the USA, there is little surprise over why the Reds chose America as the destination for their pre-season tour.

This has been quite the summer for football here and Billy Hogan, CEO of Liverpool and Fenway Sports Group (FSG), insists the aim is to build on that after what has been a "super difficult year" for the club "for lots of different reasons."

Hogan is speaking to BBC Sport in New York ahead of Andoni Iraola's side taking on Wrexham at the famous Yankee Stadium on Wednesday evening at 19:30 local time, 00:30 BST.

However, for all the excitement around a new era on the pitch, it is events off the pitch that must be addressed first.

Last week, FSG, which owns Liverpool, confirmed that a consortium led by Amit Bhatia, a British-Indian millionaire businessman, was in talks over a strategic minority investment in the club. Those talks have been ongoing and there is a growing belief that a deal will be done.

"Look, John Henry (the principal owner) and FSG have always said that if there was an interest in an investment that would help the football club, then they would consider it. That was said many years ago and that remains the case here," Hogan tells BBC Sport.

"At this point, I wouldn't say anything different to the statement that a consortium led, managed and represented by Amit Bhatia has come forward and expressed an interest in a minority investment."

Hogan, who has been with FSG since they purchased Liverpool for £300m in 2010, does stress though that they are still very much committed to the project and that news of this development should not be seen as a sign of the company, which also owns the Major League Baseball franchise, Boston Red Sox, stepping away.

According to the Financial Times, a deal with the consortium led by Bhatia would value Liverpool at more than £4.5bn.

"There's a huge opportunity still," Hogan says. "This is the biggest and most popular sport in the world and we're one of the biggest clubs in the biggest league in the biggest sport in the world. So that's a great place for us to be. The Premier League has a tremendous amount of momentum behind it.

"We've definitely not peaked. We're in a good place to continue to grow and that's why everyone across both sides of the club, football and business and whether they kick a ball or not, is focused on driving the club forward and winning trophies.

"On the pitch, our goal every season is to win trophies. Off the pitch, our priority is to continue driving overall revenues and expand and build the club.

"We're really happy with the trajectory and direction of the club - we were fifth in the Deloitte Football Money League and had the highest revenue (£702m) in the Premier League.

"All of that investment, as has always been the case since 2010, goes back into the club. It's about running the club sustainably."

Who is potential investor Bhatia?

Consortium in talks to buy Liverpool minority stake

After a record summer spend last season of £450m, Liverpool were disappointing on the pitch.

Ultimately, that led to the sacking of Arne Slot at the end of the campaign. Senior players like Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate all left on free transfers too.

It has been a summer of change at Liverpool with Michael Edwards stepping down as FSG's CEO of football, primarily because plans of multi-club ownership were abandoned.

Meanwhile, Richard Hughes, Liverpool's sporting director, is linked with a move to Al Hilal in Saudi Arabia. There is certainly a question of stability.

"Transition and change is inevitable in football. In our case, with a new coach coming in, there's real excitement around Andoni's mindset and philosophy that supporters will really enjoy," says Hogan.

"That will take time but in terms of transition, I would send a message that we are in a very healthy place as a football club - the leadership from ownership is in a very steady place and we're looking forward to the next season and the season ahead."

Hogan insists that regardless of the personnel changes, the club model remains the same and they will continue to stick to their principles.

"It's important to keep in mind that last season, a considerable amount was invested but also generated in terms of sales of players going out," he says. "Over the course of FSG's stewardship, the investment has always been focused on doing what's best to put us in a place to win.

"Sometimes that means significant expense and other times it doesn't like in the summer of 2024 when there was only one addition (Federico Chiesa for £12.5m). It depends on where we are at the club and the improvements needed. Ultimately Mike Gordon, who is really our managing owner, will make those decisions."

There is an increased focus on the women's team too, who finished 11th in the WSL last season and haven't won the top-flight title since 2014.

"To be self-critical, that is probably an area that we maybe took our eye off the ball several years ago but we've changed that," says Hogan.

"We now have one of the best training centres at AXA Melwood, we are investing in the squad and we will approach the women's team the same way we approach the men's team - which is to run it sustainably. There's tremendous growth in the women's game and a huge opportunity going forward to really drive that."

Liverpool preparing opening bid for PSG's Barcola

It is still remarkable to think now that the club was on the verge of administration when FSG took over in 2010.

It hasn't all been plain sailing. As recently as this year, Hogan wrote to fans over ticket price increases. The club cut the size of their planned rise in ticket prices for the next couple of seasons after fan protests.

However, under FSG's stewardship, Anfield has been transformed, with two of the four stands developed in the last decade.

"Back when FSG acquired LFC, a number of similarities were drawn with Boston Red Sox and Liverpool and one of them was this idea of an iconic venue that truly sits in the community," says Hogan. "One of the things we're focused on now is making improvements in the footprint around Anfield the neighbourhood whether that's infrastructure or transport and getting people in on non-match days. We're proud of how we've expanded while keeping the soul but also modernising it in the way that's befitting of the football club.

"Football doesn't give you much time to sit back and reflect. What I would say I am most proud of is that the club is in such a positive and good financial position. If you go back to that point in 2010, the club was literally on the brink of bankruptcy. Now it has the right foundations underneath it. There's improvements across the infrastructure, the ability to stay at Anfield for the long-term and the stuff that doesn't always get headlines but are super important for the health of the club.

"Ultimately, it's about winning trophies and I wish we could win more but we've been fortunate to win a few.

"I think our supporters have had a great time and I often think about the fan parks at the Champions League finals - we lost a couple but just that joy and the memories and frankly the fun of it is what I look back from time to time. And it's something that everyone associated with Liverpool should be proud of because it happens together and we all want this club to be the best in the world."

After a torrid year for Liverpool, where better to start looking ahead than in New York, the city of dreams?
